#5682. Katy Perry’s Proposed Youth Summer Camp Sparks Wildfire Concern From Santa Barbara Residents

Katy Perry’s Firework Foundation has proposed a youth summer camp just outside of her hometown of Santa Barbara, CA, but nearly 400 residents are opposing the plan, citing a laundry list of concerns from wildfire risk to traffic and noise.

According to the project’s website, Gratitude Canyon “would provide a permanent home for Camp Firework” at a Goleta property that formerly operated as the headquarters of Bragg Live Food Products—the company that popularized apple cider vinegar.

Gratitude Canyon explains that the pop star and her sister, Angela Lerche—the foundation’s president—spent “significant time” at the proposed site of the camp growing up, noting a “close friendship” with Patricia Bragg, the company’s former CEO who died in 2023 at the age of 94.

The foundation estimates that “approximately 97% of the roughly 110-acre property would remain open space, agriculture or landscaping,” and that the camp’s activity would be “concentrated on about 16 acres,” leaving “much” of the existing apple orchard to remain.

The County of Santa Barbara's Major Condition Use Permit Application Project Description supports those claims.

The program has operated for seven years across more than a dozen camp sites, and serves children ages 11 through 13, combining “art, nature, leadership, and relationship-building for young people who may not otherwise have access to immersive camp experiences.”

A petition under the name “Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon” has garnered 396 signatures from concerned residents in response to the way the project is “currently proposed.”

“The Firework Foundation is seeking County approval to rezone 183 Winchester Canyon with a General Plan Amendment and build a youth camp/event center, bringing 8,000+ visitors a year into a quiet, residential canyon, with amplified noise permitted 9am-9pm, 400-person events, and one way in or out of a high fire-risk, debris-flow zone,” the petition states.

Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon has organized the neighbors’ “top concerns.” The first on the list is that they believe the camp is a “Trojan Horse” and is a “year-round event center” designed “under the guise of a summer camp for underserved kids.”

However, Gratitude Canyon has stated that the proposal is not intended to serve as “a wedding or concert venue,” and plans to keep limited use outside of summer camp to schools, nonprofits, and “occasional retreats,” as well as “no more than four special events per year.”

Additionally, the petition raises concerns about fire safety, claiming “a formal fire protection plan and independent county-reviewed evacuation analysis still haven’t been completed,” and that evacuation capacity for the camp’s children and staff should be established prior to changing the property’s zoning.

However, Gratitude Canyon’s frequently asked questions page notes “fire prevention has been incorporated into the project form the earliest planning stages” and claim “measures include defensible space, vegetation management, emergency access, onsite water, hardened structures, evacuation planning, emergency communications, and 24-hour staffing while campers are onsite.”

The Gratitude Canyon website also explains that the Firework Foundation is engaging “directly with neighbors” and that the project “remains an evolving proposal.”

The summer camp proposal is not the first time Perry has been involved in a dispute centered around property in Santa Barbara.

The “California Gurls” singer and her former fiance, Orlando Bloom, were involved in a yearslong courtroom battle regarding a $15 million Montecito mansion.

The legal drama began in 2020, when the couple purchased the home from 1-800-Flowers founder, Carl Westcott, who rescinded the deal days later.

Westcott had reportedly purchased the estate for $11 million just two months prior, and sued Perry’s long-time business manager, Bernie Gudvi, who handled the purchase. Westcott claimed he “lacked capacity” to sell his home because he was suffering from a brain disorder and was under the influence of painkillers.

After years of legal back-and-forth, a 2023 ruling concluded that the original sale contract should be upheld. Perry countersued Westcott, seeking nearly $6 million in damages from the veteran, including $3.5 million in lost rental income and more than $2 million in repairs due to his alleged “lack of maintenance” of the property. The damages were later revised to $4.8 million.

Perry was awarded $1.94 million in damages, which was deducted from the $6 million that remained outstanding on the property’s original purchase price, leaving Perry and her representatives responsible for paying just over $4 million.

In October of this year, Westcott alleged he had only received a fraction of the amount owed, leaving Perry and Bloom susceptible to another legal confrontation.

#5680. A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength

A simple daily fiber supplement may offer a surprising new way to relieve knee arthritis pain while improving muscle strength. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham, people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) who took a prebiotic fiber called inulin experienced significant reductions in pain, improved grip strength, and decreased sensitivity to pain.

The supplement also appeared to be considerably easier for participants to stick with than a digital physical therapy program. Only 3.6% of those assigned to inulin alone dropped out of the study, compared with 21% of those assigned to physical therapy alone.

Published in the journal Nutrients, the findings suggest that improving gut health could become an additional strategy for managing arthritis. They also reveal an intriguing connection between the bacteria living in our digestive system, the way our bodies process pain, and muscle function.

A Simple Dietary Change Could Help Relieve Arthritis Pain

Knee osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and is a major cause of chronic pain and disability, especially among older adults. The condition develops as the tissues within the knee joint, including the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorate. This can lead to pain, stiffness, swelling, and difficulty with everyday activities such as walking or climbing stairs.

Treatment typically focuses on reducing symptoms and maintaining mobility. Pain medications can provide relief but may cause unwanted side effects, while physical therapy and regular exercise can help improve joint function. However, keeping up with an exercise program can be difficult, particularly for people already struggling with persistent pain.

The new research raises the possibility that a simple dietary supplement could provide another way to manage symptoms.

"This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change -- adding a fiber supplement to your breakfast or yogurt -- could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function," said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki, lead author of the study from the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham.

The supplement tested in the study was inulin, a naturally occurring fiber found in foods such as chicory root, Jerusalem artichokes, and certain other vegetables. Unlike many nutrients, inulin is not broken down by digestive enzymes in the small intestine. Instead, it passes into the large intestine, where beneficial bacteria can use it as food.

How Gut Bacteria May Influence Arthritis Pain

Researchers are increasingly discovering that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influences much more than digestion. These microbes interact with the immune system, produce biologically active compounds, and may even affect how the nervous system responds to pain.

Inulin is classified as a prebiotic because it nourishes certain beneficial gut bacteria rather than directly supplying living microorganisms, as probiotics do.

When bacteria ferment inulin, they produce substances known as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). One of the most important is butyrate, a compound that helps support the intestinal lining and can influence inflammation and biological pathways involved in pain.

The researchers found that participants taking inulin had increased levels of butyrate, suggesting that the supplement was influencing activity within the gut microbiome.

They also observed higher levels of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite and has also been linked to pain regulation and muscle health.

GLP-1 has attracted widespread attention because it is the hormone targeted by medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. However, the inulin supplement used in this trial was not a GLP-1 medication. Instead, researchers examined whether supporting beneficial gut bacteria could influence the body's own production of the hormone.

One particularly interesting finding was that higher GLP-1 levels were associated with better grip strength. Although this does not establish that GLP-1 caused the improvement, it suggests that changes originating in the digestive system may be connected to muscle function as well as pain.

To investigate these effects, the researchers conducted the INSPIRE trial, a six-week randomized controlled study involving 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis.

Participants were assigned to one of four treatment groups: a daily inulin supplement alone, digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE) alone, a combination of inulin and physical therapy, or a placebo.

This design allowed researchers to examine the effects of the supplement and exercise separately, as well as investigate whether combining them offered additional benefits.

Both inulin and physical therapy independently reduced knee pain, indicating that each approach provided meaningful symptom relief.

However, the supplement produced additional improvements that were not observed with physical therapy alone. Participants taking inulin demonstrated better grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity.

Pain sensitivity reflects how strongly the nervous system responds to potentially painful stimulation. Reducing that sensitivity could be particularly valuable for people with osteoarthritis, because persistent pain is not always explained by the amount of visible damage within a joint. Changes in how the nervous system processes pain can also contribute to discomfort.

The improved grip strength was another unexpected result, suggesting that the supplement's effects might extend beyond the knee itself.

The researchers also found a substantial difference in how many participants completed their assigned treatments. Only 3.6% of the inulin-only group dropped out, compared with 21% of the physical therapy-only group.

This difference suggests that taking a daily fiber supplement may be easier to incorporate into a regular routine than following a structured exercise program.

A Surprising Connection Between Gut Health, Muscles, and Pain

Dr. Kouraki said: "Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. The very low dropout rate compared to the exercise group is also encouraging from a public health perspective -- people were able to fit this supplement easily into their daily lives."

Beyond the reduction in arthritis pain, the researchers are particularly interested in what the findings reveal about interactions between the digestive system, muscles, and nervous system.

The association between GLP-1 and grip strength raises the possibility of a broader biological relationship connecting gut health with physical performance and resilience as people age.

Senior author Professor Ana Valdes from the School of Medicine added: "The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation. This could have implications not just for osteoarthritis, but for understanding how gut health influences aging and physical resilience more broadly."

The findings are promising, but the trial was relatively small and lasted only six weeks. Larger studies with longer follow-up periods will be needed to establish whether the benefits persist, identify which patients are most likely to respond, and clarify the biological mechanisms responsible.

The results also do not suggest that fiber supplements should replace exercise or other established arthritis treatments. Instead, they point toward a potentially useful additional approach that could complement existing care.

The potential importance of this research becomes clearer when considering how many people live with persistent arthritis pain.

Professor Lucy Donaldson, Director of Research at Arthritis UK, said: "The pain of arthritis can severely impact quality of life. Our recent lived experience survey showed that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis.

"Researchers are starting to explore the role of the gut microbiome in our experience of pain. This exciting preliminary research highlights how diet and physiotherapy can act in different ways to have benefits for people with arthritis. We know a variety and balance of healthy foods, including fiber, and regular physical activity matter, and we're glad to be supporting research that explores how they work to help people with arthritis."

For people living with knee osteoarthritis, the findings offer an encouraging possibility: a relatively simple change in daily nutrition may help reduce pain while supporting other aspects of physical health.

Perhaps most intriguingly, the research suggests that treating arthritis may involve looking beyond the joints themselves. By exploring how gut bacteria influence inflammation, pain perception, and muscle function, scientists may uncover new ways to manage a condition that affects millions of people every day.

#5679. Ballot measures affirm divisions over abortion and transgender issues

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

The blue wave that handed Democrats power in both the House and Senate did not filter neatly through ballot measures across the country.

Measures on abortion, marijuana, science funding, and Medicaid largely reflected a more liberal national sentiment. But multiple states voted to implement or enhance restrictions on transgender youth.

In Arizona, Colorado, and Washington, voters approved or were poised to approve measures to enact or expand prohibitions on transgender youth participation on school athletics teams aligned with their gender identity. Colorado also was on track to approve a new ban on gender-affirming surgery for minors.

While critics called the measures on transgender rights “ballot candy” for Republicans, there was no correlation between the measures and winning candidates’ affiliations. Colorado Democrats, for example, won the Senate, most House seats, and both the governor and attorney general offices.

The results indicate that many voters are concerned about gender, sports, and fairness in particular, but those worries may be outsized compared to the number of young transgender people these laws will apply to. Existing data suggest around 300,000 youth ages 13 to 17 nationally identify as transgender, and 40% may participate in sports. In late 2024, the NCAA said that there were fewer than 10 transgender athletes among more than 500,000 total. And in response to a recent poll, an NCAA representative confirmed that zero transgender athletes currently compete in women’s leagues.

Data is limited and murky on the physical advantage that transgender women may have in various competitions, but research so far does not suggest any inherent edge. When it comes to medical care, data show that top surgery is rare among minors, while bottom surgery on a minor’s genitals is already virtually nonexistent.

The Trump administration has relentlessly targeted youth gender-affirming care in the last two years, leading many hospitals to stop providing care like puberty blockers and hormones, even in states where the care is still legal. It’s unclear what that fight will look like now, as candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico, who have expressed support for transgender youth, won across the country. Locally, six transgender candidates won seats in state legislatures that have never previously elected transgender representatives.

“The voters rejected the anti-trans rhetoric used against candidates while still stripping away our rights at the ballot,” Chase Strangio, who leads the ACLU’s LGBT & HIV Project, said on Instagram. Strangio argued that ballot measures are “a function of funding more than anything” and should not be used as justification for more restrictive legislation.

The blue wave could have trickle-down effects on Colorado’s ballot measures. Both proposals are statutory changes, which means that even once they officially pass, the state legislature can make amendments before enacting them. On Wednesday, the state’s governor-elect said the restrictions would need “a long, hard look,” before implementation, The Denver Post reported.

Four states voted on ballot measures related to abortion, and all preserved the existing legal status.

The most contentious vote was in Missouri, where just two years ago voters narrowly approved a measure to enshrine the right to reproductive freedom in the constitution. The state legislature asked voters to reverse that decision, tying a potential abortion ban to a more popular proposal to constitutionally ban gender-affirming care for minors. (That care is already illegal in the state, but not constitutionally prohibited.) Voters rejected the bid, with nearly 56% of the vote against it.

In Nevada and Virginia, where abortion is already legal, strong majorities voted to enshrine that right in the state constitutions. Four years after the Supreme Court overruled Roe v. Wade, 26 states have some type of legal protections on abortion.

But stalwart red Idaho denied the right to abortion, preserving the state’s existing ban.

A measure to repeal Massachusetts’ recreational marijuana law was defeated handily, with nearly 76% of voters choosing to keep the grass growing. Polling showed the measure had little chance of passing, yet out of the state’s nine ballot questions, it became the most expensive. The measure was almost entirely funded by Smart Approaches to Marijuana, a national nonprofit that advocates against legalization that put $3.7 million into the campaign. Opponents paid $2.8 million.

While no other states considered measures to legalize drugs like marijuana or psychedelics, Idaho voters preserved their right to do so in the future. More than 66% rejected a proposal that would have given all power to legalize psychoactive drugs to the legislature.

But results on other drug policy measures seem to complicate the narrative of a big blue wave. Voters in two states approved measures that appear to endorse the Trump administration’s punitive approach to drug policy from his executive order naming fentanyl as a weapon of mass destruction. Arizona approved a measure naming drug cartels terrorist organizations and directing the state’s Department of Homeland Security to address the threat, while Colorado voted to increase criminal penalties for the possession, manufacture, and sale of fentanyl. (Colorado’s governor-elect said this, too, may need to be reconsidered.)

Golden State voters appeared on track to pass California’s Proposition 38, which authorizes $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research. The result suggests that the state’s voters were eager to defend research funding after the Trump administration’s slew of grant terminations, delays, and disruptions. But the measure has generated controversy because of where that funding will likely go.

Prop 38 will direct half the funds, $4.2 billion, to a single institute that isn’t named explicitly but which must meet a long list of criteria that experts in California politics call “oddly specific.” Only one institute appears to meet those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy. This institute, also known as CIII, was cofounded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist, retired surgeon, and Prop 38’s leading backer. Michelson poured more than $40 million of his own money into the Yes on 38 campaign; fellow CIII co-founder and treasure Meyer Luskin contributed $5 million in support of the measure. As of mid-October, the “No on 38” campaign had raised less than $9,000.

CIII is still under construction and went from having zero employees during the 2024 calendar year to three last month, according to documents filed with the Internal Revenue Service and reporting by CalMatters. STAT’s own reporting revealed that the American Association of Immunologists, the field’s leading scientific society, seriously considered pulling its endorsement of Prop 38 once it became clear half the funds would likely go to Michelson’s institute. The organization decided to maintain support after its governing body met with Michelson in August.

The measure also drew support from more than 70 organizations, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the state’s Democratic and Republican parties.

Proponents argued that this investment would help researchers working to cure or treat new treatments for Alzheimer’s, heart disease, and cancer. They also framed Prop 38 as a way for voters to protect California from abrupt turns in federal science funding.

Other health-related ballot initiatives saw mixed results, reflecting voters’ overarching concern with affordability and funding.

As national Medicaid cuts loom, South Dakota voters rejected an amendment that would have conditioned the state’s expansion program — already approved by voters — on the federal share of funding remaining at 90%. Proponents of the measure argued that decreases in federal funding would make it too expensive for the state. But it also would have meant a sudden loss of coverage for the tens of thousands of residents who are enrolled through the expansion program.

Arizona voters approved a measure to require voter approval for any local taxes on groceries, and to cap any such tax at 2%. (There’s no statewide sales tax on groceries, but local jurisdictions can enact them.)

North Dakota voters narrowly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to require public schools to offer all students free breakfast and lunch. The program would have cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years, per the North Dakota Monitor.

The result threatens to complicate Trump’s push for clearer crypto regulations. Bitcoin price weakness now reflects both market risk aversion and concerns that Congress could delay legislation designed to establish a federal framework for digital assets.

Bitcoin briefly dropped more than $2,000 after early election results pointed toward a Democratic victory, falling from nearly $78,000 to the $75,000 level. Buyers subsequently stepped in, lifting BTC toward $77,700 this morning.

The immediate risk is that negotiations become slower and more complicated, leaving crypto firms without the regulatory clarity they have sought.

Bitcoin price direction will likely depend on whether the election-driven selloff spreads into a deeper market correction. A sustained recovery in Nasdaq could help Bitcoin regain momentum, particularly if investors begin treating the election result as a temporary source of uncertainty rather than a lasting threat to risk assets.

On the other hand, continued weakness in technology stocks could pressure BTC and altcoins further. Investors will also watch whether Democrats pursue aggressive investigations or push for substantial changes to crypto legislation.

The political shift could create a more difficult environment for Trump’s crypto agenda during the final two years of his presidency. Yet a divided government may also limit sweeping policy changes from either party.

For now, Bitcoin price remains caught between broader market weakness and uncertainty over U.S. crypto regulation. The election has changed the political landscape, but the next moves in Congress will determine whether the impact becomes a lasting obstacle for the industry.

#5676. A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body

A single sauna session may trigger a surprising response in the immune system. Researchers in Finland have discovered that spending just 30 minutes in a sauna, with a brief cold shower halfway through, causes white blood cells to surge into the bloodstream. These cells are essential to the body's defenses, helping identify and fight infections and other potential threats.

The findings suggest that sauna bathing may temporarily mobilize immune cells that normally remain in tissues, allowing them to circulate more widely throughout the body. This increased movement could help the immune system monitor for harmful pathogens, including bacteria and viruses.

During the study, researchers observed an increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured. Among them were neutrophils and lymphocytes, two important groups of immune cells. Neutrophils are often among the first defenders to respond to an infection, while lymphocytes include cells that recognize specific threats, produce antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses.

The increase was temporary. Within 30 minutes after the sauna session, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts had returned to their original levels.

How Sauna Bathing May Activate Immune Defenses

"This may indicate that sauna bathing mobilizes additional white blood cells into the bloodstream from tissues, where they are then redeposited after the session. This kind of periodic release of white blood cells into the bloodstream is beneficial, as once they leave their storage sites, they are better able to patrol the body and respond to pathogens," says Ilkka Heinonen, an Academy Research Fellow at the University of Turku.

This process is known as immune surveillance. Rather than remaining in one location, immune cells travel through the bloodstream and tissues, searching for signs of infection or other abnormalities. By temporarily increasing the number of white blood cells in circulation, the body may improve their ability to detect potential threats.

Interestingly, a similar response occurs during physical exercise. Exercise can temporarily increase the number of immune cells moving through the bloodstream, helping distribute them throughout the body. The new findings suggest that sauna bathing may produce a comparable short-term response, although this does not mean the two activities provide identical immune benefits.

Sauna Heat Also Affects Immune Signaling Molecules

The researchers also investigated whether sauna bathing influenced cytokines, small proteins that help immune cells communicate with one another. Cytokines play important roles in regulating inflammation, coordinating immune defenses, and directing the body's response to infections.

Overall, the sauna session produced little change in average cytokine levels in the bloodstream. However, a closer examination revealed an interesting connection between certain cytokines and changes in body temperature.

"Interestingly, however, the levels of several cytokines changed in relation to how much body temperature rose during sauna bathing. No similar association was observed between white blood cell counts and changes in body temperature," says Professor Jari Laukkanen, who led the study at the University of Eastern Finland.

In other words, some immune signaling molecules responded differently depending on how much a person's body temperature increased. White blood cell counts, however, did not show the same relationship with rising body temperature.

This distinction suggests that sauna bathing may influence different parts of the immune system through different physiological processes.

What This Discovery Means for Sauna Health Benefits

Previous research has linked regular sauna bathing with several potential health benefits. The latest findings offer another clue about what may be happening inside the body during these sessions, particularly how heat exposure and the sauna routine affect immune cell circulation.

However, the researchers caution that the results do not establish whether sauna bathing produces lasting improvements in immune function or reduces the risk of illness. The study examined only the immediate effects of one sauna session, and the observed changes in white blood cells were short-lived.

Because the session also included a brief cold shower, the findings reflect the combined sauna and cooling routine rather than the isolated effects of heat alone.

The research involved 51 adults with an average age of 50. The findings were published in the scientific journal Temperature, which specializes in research on body temperature regulation and its effects on human physiology.

Although more research is needed to understand the long-term implications, the study reveals that even a single sauna session can rapidly change how immune cells circulate through the body, potentially offering new insight into the biological effects of this popular relaxation practice.

#5675. Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay

Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.

Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health.

Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health.

How Cranberry Juice Affects Harmful Bacteria

Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells.

Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities.

Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume.

"Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said.

To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water.

"It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.

On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth.

After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing.

Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period.

A Surprising Effect on Plaque and Tooth Decay

The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples.

Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities.

The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids.

Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context.

"Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said.

Could Cranberry Juice Become Part of Oral Care?

Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health.

Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay.

Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness.

"But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable."

The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#5673. Beyond the Zero Down Payment: The Best States for Homebuyers Using VA Loans in 2026

VA loans can help veterans and active-duty service members turn their dream of homeownership into a reality.

Partly guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, they don’t require down payments or charge monthly mortgage insurance, unlike many other loan programs.

If you or a loved one are eligible for a VA loan, you may be wondering where to buy a home. According to Military.com, Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee are all solid options.

“What makes these states attractive isn't necessarily one standout benefit. It's the combination of things that can make life after the military a little easier, whether that's keeping more of your retirement income, finding a good civilian job, or living somewhere with a strong veteran community,” says Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight at Veterans United Home Loans in Columbia, MO.

By becoming familiar with what each state has to offer, you could narrow down your home search and find a property that aligns with your lifestyle budget.

From no property taxes and lower housing costs to veteran-specific tax breaks, these military-friendly states can make homeownership more accessible and affordable.

According to data from the VA, Virginia is one of the leading states for VA-backed loans, likely due to its large military population and steady real estate market growth.

“Northern Virginia’s proximity to government facilities like the Pentagon, Fort Belvoir, and Marine Corps Base Quantico allows many veterans to transition into federal or defense-related employment without uprooting their families,” says Dell Jeanty, real estate agent at Dell Residential in Arlington, VA.

The state offers real estate tax exemption for qualifying veterans with a 100% service-connected, permanent and total disability. Additionally, due to the major military installations and frequent military relocations, Virginia has a high concentration of assumable loans.

“This means you could potentially take over a seller's lower, locked-in historical interest rate and further your savings as a veteran,” Jeanty adds.

Many markets in North Carolina, including Charlotte, offer opportunities for veterans at different stages of life, whether you’re transitioning to a civilian career or retiring.

“There’s an established veteran community and plenty of ways to build new connections through work, recreation, and shared interests. You can choose city living or quieter settings with more land while enjoying professional sports, outdoor activities, and travel access,” says Ashley Horton, global real estate adviser at Premier Sotheby's International Realty in Charlotte.

Also, military installations across the Carolinas like Fort Liberty and Camp Lejeune are within driving distance, and highway connections and a major airport keep you connected to other markets. Plus, North Carolina lets qualifying military retirees deduct military retirement pay from state taxable income.

“Compared with markets in other states, those in North Carolina can give you more home, more space, and more options for the same budget. If you’re relocating from higher-cost cities, the equity from your previous home can stretch further here,” adds Horton.

Florida is one of those states where you’ll never run out of things to do.

You can enjoy country living with land and wide-open spaces, a coastal environment with beautiful beaches and waterways, or a neighborhood close to shopping, restaurants, and entertainment. And of course, you can’t beat being able to enjoy the outdoors almost year-round.

“I live and sell in the Orlando area, which is most well known for the Disney and Universal theme parks. In fact, Universal Studios Orlando just opened the Epic Universe park—fun for the whole family,” says Christina Rordam, a real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando.

Also, since there are fewer homebuyers to compete with in Florida, you may have more leverage to negotiate ideal terms.

According to Rordam, there are currently two groups of sellers: the motivated and the unrealistic.

“The motivated home sellers are moving for job transfers, divorcing, having kids, and needing more space. These types of life events really encourage sellers to take a long, hard look at the current market and cut buyers a good deal,” Rordam explains.

In the past, it was almost unthinkable to negotiate price, repairs, and closing costs. Now, it's much more likely.

Rordam has a cash buyer for whom she negotiated $1,600 in repairs and $20,000 off the purchase price on a home that had been on the market less than a week.

In addition, Florida has no state individual income tax and some valuable property tax benefits for qualifying veterans.

“For example, certain veterans with service-connected disabilities may qualify for additional homestead property tax exemptions, and veterans with qualifying total and permanent service–connected disabilities may be eligible for a full exemption from property taxes on their homestead. Those savings can make a real difference in the overall cost of owning a home,” says Sheena Haney, broker and owner at Haney Signature Realty in St. Augustine, FL.

To Haney, Florida is more than just a place to buy a home.

“It’s a place where you can really enjoy the lifestyle, raise a family, retire, and make lasting memories,” adds Haney.

Texas gives veteran buyers something incredibly valuable: options.

In Central Texas, for example, you’ll find everything from established neighborhoods to new construction, where builders may offer incentives to make homeownership more affordable.

“San Antonio is especially attractive because of its relatively low cost of living, allowing many military families to stretch their housing budgets further,” says April Guerra, real estate agent at LPT Realty in Leander, TX.

Put simply, the Lone Star State doesn’t force you to sacrifice space, amenities, or lifestyle to find a home within your budget.

“If you’re a veteran looking to establish roots after military service, that flexibility can make a meaningful difference,” Guerra explains.

Texas also has a long-standing connection to the military.

“I grew up in San Antonio, proudly known as Military City, USA, home to Joint Base San Antonio, including Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, and Randolph. Now, working in the Austin area, I'm also near Camp Mabry and Fort Hood. Military families are an important part of these communities,” says Guerra.

There’s an established VA healthcare system as well.

“For example, in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, Dallas has a full-service VA hospital.  Fort Worth has a large VA outpatient clinic,” says Elizabeth Lane, real estate agent at HomeSmart Realty in Dallas.

Additionally, Texas offers no state individual income tax, potential property tax exemptions for qualifying disabled veterans, and access to military and veteran support networks.

There's also a strong sense of community and diverse employment opportunities.

“Companies like Lockheed Martin and Bell Textron have a large presence in North Texas and like to recruit veterans,” adds Lane.

Tennessee offers a unique mix of benefits for military homebuyers.

First and foremost, there’s no state income tax.

“On top of that, Tennessee has some of the lowest property taxes in the U.S., ranking roughly eighth to 10th lowest, depending on the specific index,” says Wendy Monday, real estate agent at Broker Onward Real Estate in Nashville, TN.

By contrast, states such as New Jersey and Illinois have significantly higher tax rates, which add considerably to the cost of homeownership.

Also, Nashville is one of the premier healthcare hubs in the country, making top-quality medical care exceptionally accessible locally.

It boasts an incredibly high density of Level 1 Trauma Centers, top-tier children's hospitals, and specialized emergency rooms right in the metro area.

“You won't have to travel to another city or state if you or a family member ever face a complex diagnosis or require a rare medical specialist,” Monday explains.

#5672. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

#5671. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

#5668. EXCLUSIVE: ‘The Wolves of Real Estate’ Director Reveals the Unanswered Questions Behind the Alexander Brothers’ Downfall

Before their names became synonymous with a federal sex-trafficking case, Tal and Oren Alexander built careers selling some of the country’s most expensive homes.

Now, a documentary examining the brothers and their crimes is raising questions about the role wealth, professional prestige, and exclusive social circles played in giving them access to women.

Peacock’s three-part series, “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” examines the rise and downfall of Tal, Oren, and their brother Alon, tracing a story that stretched from luxury properties and lavish parties to a Manhattan courtroom.

All three were convicted of federal sex offenses, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, on March 9. On Oct. 27, each was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Emma Schwartz, director of “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” says the brothers’ status helped draw women into their orbit, while cautioning against assuming that every allegation involved their professional lives.

“Testimony at trial made clear that the brothers’ wealth and status was one of the reasons they were able to attract so many women,” Schwartz says.

“But many of the allegations we heard about did not involve their jobs or work.”

Tal and Oren rose to prominence at Douglas Elliman before leaving in 2022 to co-found luxury brokerage Official.

Their résumés included the $238 million Manhattan penthouse transaction at 220 Central Park South in 2019, which set a U.S. residential sale record at the time. Alon, Oren’s twin, worked in the family’s private security business.

Prosecutors described a scheme in which the brothers used their money and connections, including Tal and Oren’s standing in ultraluxury real estate, to facilitate sexual assaults.

Women were enticed with trips, accommodations, and exclusive experiences, according to the government’s account of the evidence.

Yet the criminal proceedings were not primarily an examination of the brokerage business, Schwartz explains.

“One of the interesting things about the criminal trial was how little it focused on the brothers’ professional lives,” Schwartz says.

Only one Douglas Elliman agent testified, according to the interview responses, with the government seeking information about a summer lease in the Hamptons.

Nevertheless, some testimony revealed an overlap between the properties associated with the brothers’ business image and the places where women said they were assaulted.

“For instance, the house that two women testified at trial that they were raped and trafficked to, was featured in a business video for the brothers,” Schwartz says.

Another woman testified that the possibility of making a professional connection had interested her in attending a party to which the brothers had invited her friend, according to Schwartz.

Those accounts illustrate how professional opportunity and social access could intersect. They do not, on their own, establish that the brothers systematically used access to clients’ listings to commit crimes.

Questions about what others knew also remain central to the story.

“One of the biggest questions so many have is who knew what about the brothers’ behavior?” Schwartz says.

The interview responses point to an email from an Elliman official, discussed in the documentary and presented at trial, as evidence that at least some people knew about the brothers’ playboy lifestyle.

But Schwartz distinguishes that awareness from knowledge of sexual violence.

“We also know from reporters at The Real Deal that there had been rumors about the brothers’ alleged behavior circulating in the industry for years before the lawsuits came out,” Schwartz says.

Rumors, awareness of partying, and evidence that a particular person knew about a crime are different matters. The responses do not establish criminal wrongdoing by the brokerage or its other employees.

For Schwartz, another striking aspect of the trial was the difficulty women described in acknowledging and reporting their experiences.

“One of the striking things about the trial was how so many of the women said they had been ashamed and too afraid to report what happened to them,” Schwartz says.

Some took months or years to describe what happened as rape or sexual assault, according to the interview responses.

That hesitation is a significant part of the documentary’s larger story: the barriers women faced in coming forward, even as the brothers maintained wealth and social standing.

“This all raises an important issue about sexual assault cases: women often take a long time, sometimes years, before they are ready to speak about what happened,” Schwartz says.

The civil justice system also played a role. New York’s Adult Survivors Act created a temporary window allowing adults to bring certain sexual-assault claims that would otherwise have been barred by expired filing deadlines. That window ran from Nov. 24, 2022 through Nov. 24, 2023.

Schwartz credits that law with allowing the first two women to file their civil claims, helping set in motion the public scrutiny that followed.

“This is a story about why speaking up matters,” Schwartz says.

“It took just two women filing lawsuits, amplified by the media to open the floodgates for dozens of women to come forward.”

Asked whether the case reveals something broader about luxury brokerages, Schwartz resists drawing a sweeping conclusion about the entire industry.

“It’s really hard to know how much anyone can generalize from the brothers to the industry more broadly.”

The hope, instead, is that the women’s accounts will help others feel able to share their own experiences.

“The women and people who spoke for our documentary did so in hopes that sharing their experience would encourage others to speak up and not feel the shame they did.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5667. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

Indeed, Americans were broadly concerned about affordability in the months leading up to the election. While Trump said he remained focused on it, he spent the run-up to the election detailing projects in Washington, DC, such as a botched effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

#5664. The Renovation Cool-Off Is Here, but Delaying Certain Repairs Could Cost You More Than You Save

Spending on home improvements and repairs is only expected to grow by 1.5% by the third quarter of 2027, according to Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies. Given the high cost of labor and materials these days, this is no surprise.

But if you’re trying to cut back on home projects to save some cash, it's important to understand which ones are truly optional and which ones actually need immediate attention.

“Not every project needs to happen right away. Your home doesn't have to look brand-new to be safe, comfortable, and in good shape,” says Jeri Goodkin Dausey, president and certified general contractor at SBC in Miami Beach, FL.

By knowing how to prioritze your budget, you can protect your home’s condition and value without draining your savings.

There are quite a few projects you can delay without hurting your home, as long as everything is safe and working properly.

“Sometimes, waiting can save you quite a bit of money in the short term,” Dausey explains.

Here’s what you can put on the back burner until you have more funds at your disposal.

If your cabinets, countertops, and fixtures are still in decent shape and everything works, there's no need to rush into a complete remodel.

“Let's say you were planning to spend $25,000 on a renovation but could take care of the immediate issue with a $500 repair instead. That's $24,500 you can hold onto for now,” says Dausey.

A fresh coat of paint or new trim can make a significant difference in your home’s aestehtics, but these are usually things that can wait if the walls and surfaces are in good shape.

“If you put off a $4,000 paint job and just spend $200 on a few touch-ups, you've kept another $3,800 in your budget,” Dausey explains.

Dmitri Popescu, general manager at Olympic Decks in Seattle, echoes Dausey’s thoughts.

“Repainting a room because you dislike the color or replacing an undamaged backsplash can generally wait. There’s no need to spend your money on a temporary makeover,” Popescu explains.

Not loving the look of your floors doesn't necessarily mean you need to replace them. If they're safe, stable, and free of water damage, you may be able to live with them a little longer.

“Putting off an $8,000 replacement and spending $300 on maintenance leaves you with $7,700. Just be sure to check out loose tiles, soft spots or areas that are lifting,” says Dausey.

An outdoor kitchen, new landscaping, or a bigger patio might be nice to have, but they're not necessities. If everything outside is safe and in good shape, these projects can wait.

“Delaying a $15,000 cosmetic upgrade in your backyard frees up a lot of money for other things. Just don't overlook problems like poor drainage, hazardous trees, or an unsafe deck,” advises Dausey.

These expert tips can help you decide whether a project can wait:

Ask yourself, does this project actually protect my home, or is it simply for aesthetics?

“Cosmetic upgrades can wait, but projects that protect the structural integrity and long-term value of your property can't,” says Roxanne Conrad, chief operating officer at Premium Service Brands in Charlottesville, VA.

Clogged gutters and unstable exterior surfaces like missing shingles and unsealed windows, for example, can be an issue.

“They can lead to much larger problems down the road if neglected for too long,” Conrad says.

If you’ve noticed the issue a while ago and it’s worsening, it likely deserves your time and money.

“Catching problems early is almost always easier and cheaper than repairing them as they fail,” Conrad explains.

Take care of what keeps your home safe, dry, and in good shape, and don't feel pressured to tackle every cosmetic project right away.

Keith Ostendorf, project developer at Next Stage Design + Build in San Jose, CA, recommends phasing.

“Some homeowners move forward in phases, which spreads out the spending and can cut the costs of moving out, since work in one part of the house can happen while the family lives in the rest,” he adds.
