#5660. Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress

Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January.

The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed.

The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump, who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence."

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

"If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula, CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com.

Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas, Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend.

Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in.

Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act.

That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts. But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level.

In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act, with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines.

Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move.

Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence.

The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding."

While data centers affect property taxes, the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open.

Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers.

"Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far."

The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions.

Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas.

It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says.

"That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5659. OpenAI to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to acquire Pierre Computer Company Inc., a low-profile developer tooling startup.

The terms of the deal were not disclosed. Observers pegged it as a shot at Microsoft Corp.’s open-source software repository GitHub for the age of artificial intelligence agents.

Pierre operates a cloud service that AI agents can use to store the code they generate. It can also store related files such as software licenses and interface design elements. According to Pierre, the service provides significantly better performance than competing technologies. It helped one customer, AI startup Lovable Inc., cut code retrieval latency by about 70%.

Pierre also develops a collection of popular open-source libraries. Two of those libraries, Trees and Diffs, underpin the interface of OpenAI’s Codex programming tool.

Large software projects contain upwards of hundreds of code files that are organized in dozens of folders. Many programming tools include a sidebar specifically designed to help developers navigate those folders. Trees, the first Pierre-developed library used by Codex, marks it easier to implement such sidebars.

Trees can equip a folder navigation sidebar with a search feature and drag-and-drop controls for moving subfolders. Additionally, it flags code files that have been recently added or updated. Developers review those files first when performing tasks such as troubleshooting an outage.

Diffs, the other Pierre library that OpenAI has integrated into Codex, is also designed to power programming tool interfaces. In particular, it can be used to implement the main interface that shows the code the user is currently editing.

When a code file is updated, Diffs points out the specific lines of code that changed to spare developers the hassle of manually finding them. It can show changes in a separate interface section or in-line.

OpenAI will continue to offer Trees and Diffs under an open-source license after the acquisition closes. Additionally, it plans to integrate the features of Pierre’s paid code hosting service into Codex. In the longer term, the Pierre team will help OpenAI “ship new products and platforms.”

The effort will place an emphasis on building software that can optimize coding agents. In particular, OpenAI hopes to streamline agent workflows that involve Git. That’s an open-source tool developers use to manage code files. Trees, Diffs and Pierre’s paid storage service all provide built-in support for Git.

OpenAI makes extensive use of the tool internally. On Monday, the company revealed that it has built a software engine called Pando to boost the performance of its internal Git environment. The engine reduces the amount of time it takes OpenAI engineers’ coding agents to create and read code files.

On a recent episode of her podcast, "Not Gonna Lie," the mom of four revealed that their daughters— Finnley, 18 months, Bennett, 3, Elliotte, 5, and Wyatt, 7—love having guests read to them.

“I know one way to my girls’ hearts, and really kids, I always tell people you don’t need to bring gifts when you come to our house. If you come in, you sit down, you offer to read our girls a book, they will be like forever," she revealed.

Kelce added, “Like genuinely, we have obviously family [that] will come and they’ll bring this and they’ll bring that, but if when you come and you sit down, you read a book, I think it’s one of the best ways to connect with kids.”

The glimpse of her houseguest request came just days after she defended her and her spouse's decision to snap up multiple Philadelphia properties right next to each other.

In an episode of her podcast, which featured guest Nikki Glaser, Kelce, 34, and the comedian chatted about hate comments.

"Do you ever get in the comments? Do you ever get feisty?” Glaser asked.

“One of the ones that I did it—which was not to a person so it doesn’t really feel as aggressive—was like ‘Celeb Homes.’ They put a bird’s-eye view of where we live with our children, and they were trying to give details of our property," she said.

We find that those are the values that we were raised with that we want our kids to have, not just because we tell them that, but because we live it," she explained.

The decision, she explained, reflects their desire to remain actively involved in their daughters' everyday lives.

Rather than bringing in someone to provide full-time care, the Kelces turn to their extended family for additional support.

Kelce said maintaining those close family relationships is particularly important because she wants her daughters to grow up with the same values that shaped her and Jason's childhoods.

#5657. United Wholesale Mortgage Pushes Through Q3 Amid Headwinds, Predicts Steady Q4

Despite having lower margins for the third quarter, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) Chairman, President and CEO Mat Ishbia stated that he feels prepared to handle “headwinds in the industry” during the company’s third quarter earnings call.

On the call, Ishbia referenced the challenges the mortgage market has faced within the past five years, saying that the market is “showing a lot of warts on a lot of different companies.”

“Everyone’s got some issue,” he stated. “A lot of other people are operating holes where they don’t have enough business. They don’t have enough opportunity to get loans, they can’t keep up production and they can’t invest in AI.”

Interest rates have weighed on the housing market heavily as of late, leaving mortgage lenders with lower demand. For UWM’s earnings however, Ishbia attributes the company’s success to the recent Oaktree partnership, which came together after an ugly bidding war with CrossCountry Mortgage.

“The best way to hedge is to do a lot more loans when rates drop, as long as you can stomach the Mortgage Servicing Right (MSR) values going down because rates drop,” Ishbia added. “We have a great hedging policy and process. We partnered with Oaktree on that and Vandy Fartaj. We feel really good about the process of how we’re hedging and how much to hedge, versus how much not to hedge.”

The latest Federal Reserve meeting in October concluded with no changes to rates, but mortgage rates have slowly begun to inch downward to the lower 7% range—around 7.24% according to Freddie Mac—after spiking dramatically from the September meeting’s rate hike.

“I think the natural hedge is the best way to do it, and we’re not back to the natural hedge yet,” he said.

Although the quarter’s loan origination volume came in at $33.4 billion—down from Q2 which was $39.7 billion, and the first quarter at $44.9 billion—Ishbia mentioned that expenses were down substantially, specifically tied into investments with AI technology.

“Those (expenses) are really just tied to the investments we’ve made in AI and technology over the last couple years when everyone thought our expenses were higher,” he noted. “And so we’re starting to see the fruits of our labor.”

In total, Q3 revenue clocked in around $811.1 million, which is down from last quarter’s $888 million and slightly down from last year’s revenue of around $843 million.

Adjusted EBITDA came in at $178.3 million, less than last quarter and last year’s estimates ($185.9 million and $211.1 million, respectively).

UWM’s stock grew following the earnings call, as the earnings report beat out expectations. The company’s stock jumped nearly 13%, but is still down about 59% year to date.

Net loss was down quarterly in Q3, to $212.6 million compared to Q2 at $451.9 million. It was significantly higher than last year’s Q3 net loss however ($12.1 million). As an improvement from the previous quarter, Ishbia again credits the lower expenses to the company’s AI investments now panning out.

“AI can definitely help you cut costs and expenses, and you’re seeing some of that benefit, but you have to make a massive investment in it to do that. As you can see, it helps you do more loans, grow your business and drive the top line revenue,” he commented.

As for market share, Ishbia emphasizes the power and role brokers play in UWM’s success. He described brokers as the “growing channel” and states that they are the “winners right now.”

“UWM’s market share is fantastic. We’re strong, we’re dominant, and we’re going to continue to grow. If we lose market share, I hope that happens because that means the broker market has gotten so big and it’s going to keep growing, that’s my focus,” he continued. “My focus is growing the broker channel, helping every loan officer do a little bit more loans, helping every real estate agent that works with brokers do more business, and helping them all win.”

With 2026 winding down, Ishbia sees the upcoming year as a time of “optimization” but said he expected the mortgage market to remain tough for some time. He also notes that UWM focuses primarily on purchase mortgages, and acknowledges the challenges that refinance mortgage loans could face with current rates.

“Since we’re mostly purchase, I’m not as concerned about the volume going down as much as a lot of refinance shops will,” he concluded. “Traditionally, the fourth quarter and first quarter are always the tougher times in the mortgage market. But once again, expenses are down, AI is winning and brokers are growing. We feel like we’re in the best position of anybody to capitalize on opportunity.”

#5656. Arista’s record quarter shows the network has become central to AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The artificial intelligence buildout is well underway, with much of the focus on silicon and compute hardware. The network is treated as plumbing, something you connect after the important decisions have been made. Arista Networks Inc.’s strong third-quarter results signaled greater awareness of the network’s critical role, and Arista is well-positioned to benefit from this secular trend.

Arista reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% year over year and 20.5% sequentially. That is the fastest growth in the company’s history as a public company and well ahead of its $3.3 billion guide. Adjusted, non-GAAP earnings per share were $1.20, up from 77 cents a year ago. Gross margin was 64%, operating margin was 49.1%, and cash totaled $14.4 billion with no debt.

Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for the fourth time this year to about $13.3 billion, representing 48% growth. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to come in between $3.9 billion and $4 billion. Arista also gave a first look at 2027, calling for 38% to 40% growth to about $18.5 billion. Within that, AI networking is expected to double from $3.5 billion to about $7 billion, and campus is expected to grow 60% to about $2 billion. The shares rose about 12% in after-hours trading, moderating to a 5% rise today.

Though investors will always gravitate toward the numbers as proof points, the commentary by Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal (pictured) was equally important. “We believe the industry is shifting from a compute-centric vertical stack to a holistic network-centric approach,” she said.

I agree, and the reason is economics. In large clusters, the network often determines how productive the AI factory is. When packets drop or a link fails, expensive accelerators sit idle, and inference makes the problem worse. Ullal described the move from “highly centralized training compute to disaggregated and distributed inference,” with prefill, decode, storage and KV cache spread across resources. “A well-designed network is becoming a foundational cornerstone for optimal token efficiency,” she said.

Buyers are getting it. Boards and chief financial officers now measure AI by cost per token and accelerator utilization, both of which depend on the network. A 5% gain in GPU utilization across a multigigawatt build is worth far more than the switches that delivered it. Once you understand that math, the network shifts from a commodity to a performance decision.

This awareness benefits every networking vendor, but it disproportionately benefits Arista for three reasons.

The first is accelerator diversity. Three years ago, Arista talked about four or five AI customers running 50,000 to 100,000 Nvidia Corp. graphics processing units, often on InfiniBand. Today, it has more than 100 Etherlink customers and expects more than 10 gigawatts of deployment across 10 or more types of accelerators by the end of 2027.

“In 2026, we are in a super cycle of AI,” Ullal said. “What a stark inflection in just three years.” Nvidia is a formidable networking competitor, and its Spectrum-X Ethernet has won over hyperscalers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Oracle Corp. But Nvidia’s networking is optimized around its own full stack, and as customers bring Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Maia, Meta MTIA, Qualcomm Corp., and Cerebras  Inc. silicon into production, many will prefer a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing accelerator.

Every new accelerator expands the share of AI networking open to an independent Ethernet vendor, and Arista leads that category. Co-design work with Cerebras and Maia means Arista is now involved in system design rather than added afterward.

The second is scale-across. Power limits are forcing AI capacity to be spread across buildings and regions, and connecting those sites requires deep buffers, large routing tables and very high reliability. Ullal said scale-across accounted for about 30% of AI demand this year and should rise in 2027, with the 7800 platform as the anchor. “There’s just no room for error when you’re connecting millions of XPUs,” she said. This is where Arista’s routing and EOS software experience matter most.

The third is scale-up. Arista showcased rack-scale Ethernet designs at OCP, built on the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking or ESUN specification, with trials in 2027 and production in 2028. Ullal compared it to the InfiniBand transition: Arista expects to move from “staring at proprietary UALink or NVLink” to “of course, it’s going to be ESUN.” If that happens, Arista’s market expands inside the rack, a segment it has never served.

Security strengthens the argument. Chief Technology Officer Ken Duda said Arista is working with Anthropic PBC, Google LLC and OpenAI Group PBC to integrate AI-driven vulnerability discovery into its software pipeline, including through Project Glasswing. As AI finds flaws faster, an operating system with process isolation and hitless patching becomes an advantage.

Ullal drew the contrast sharply: “Everybody else is dealing with a game of Whac-A-Mole where they’ve got thousands of vulnerabilities and no AVA can possibly keep track of it.” President and Chief Operating Officer Todd Nightingale said this “Glasswing and Mythos effect” is a major reason campus is growing so far ahead of the market.

The stock had fallen more than 20% in the month before the report, according to Chartmill, and analysts raised several concerns.

Deferred revenue. Total deferred revenue was flat at about $6.8 billion, which some interpret as a sign of slowing demand. CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said the balance had “the largest churn in and out” yet stayed flat while the company delivered 58.5% growth, and that the year-end balance will be higher than last year. Ullal said parsing it that way turns demand into “a physics problem,” adding, “We’re just in the best position we’ve been in a long, long time in my 18-year career at Arista.”

Spending and margins. Research and development jumped to $408.5 million from $278.1 million. Duda attributed the increase to hyperscaler prototypes and liquid cooling, and Breithaupt kept the long-term R&D range at 9% to 11% of revenue. Gross margin dipped from 65.2% a year ago, but Ullal held the long-term range at 62% to 64%, including for scale-up products.

Supply and visibility. Purchase commitments rose to $11.4 billion, and inventory to $3.2 billion. Multiyear agreements now cover silicon, circuit boards and memory. Regarding visibility, Ullal said that although Arista has two quarters of order visibility, “we have two years of work behind it.”

For several years, the debate over Arista has centered on whether Ethernet could displace InfiniBand. While InfiniBand will continue to play a key role in AI buildouts, Ethernet has much broader applicability, and its growth will outpace InfiniBand.

The new question is how much of the AI system the network will define, and this quarter suggests the answer is more than most expected. As accelerators multiply, inference spreads and AI-driven threats grow, value moves toward the layer that connects and protects everything. That is Arista’s layer.

Sebastien Naji of William Blair expressed a similar view in his earnings note. “As networking becomes a more important lever for improving performance and token output in AI data centers, Arista is well positioned to capture a growing share of spending across the most demanding AI workloads,” he wrote. “Combined with continued share gains at enterprises and neoclouds, we believe Arista’s expanding addressable market and competitive positioning support further upside in the coming quarters. We continue to view Arista as a core AI infrastructure holding and reiterate our Outperform rating.”

The biggest risk to Arista isn’t deferred revenue or market demand; it’s whether it can keep executing as crisply as it has as it gets bigger and demand accelerates But execution is something the company has excelled at under Jayshree Ullal.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5655. AI agents meet billable hours as Certinia rethinks services delivery

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky, chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE. “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier, chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to optimize renewals. Everything we’re doing is ultimately affecting the bottom line.”

Certinia’s long-time relationship with Salesforce is a key element in the company’s overall strategy. Certinia is featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce’s AgentExchange and has provided AI-powered sales and delivery for Salesforce’s consulting partner network.

“We have a deep partnership with Salesforce,” said Raju Malhotra, chief product and technology officer of Certinia. “I spend personally a lot of time with the Salesforce executives on business and engineering, and we collaborate. We bring our customer use cases, they tell us about what’s coming up from a capability perspective and we work very well together. They’re led by a founder [chief executive officer] who’s very much in tune with the market, and they want to stay ahead.”

Certinia has sought to stay ahead in its own right by introducing Veda, an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine that functions as the company’s suite of AI specialist agents and intelligent actions. The solution delivers rules-bound, trusted and ROI-focused autonomous workflows, combining Certinia’s years of institutional memory with advanced AI reasoning. Certinia’s goal with Veda is to provide customers with enough flexibility so that agents integrated into existing business workflows can drive immediate and measurable value.

“We’ve infused Veda throughout the experience for users to be more productive,” Malhotra said. “We have packaged agents, which are Veda agents. We launched Veda with 10 packages. Now we have 24, and we will finish the year with more than 40 packaged agents. Those agents are very much persona based, and they help our customers.”

Veda is not simply a layer of generic automation; it represents a key shift in how AI is being used in the enterprise. Certinia’s focus on serving the professional services market motivated the company to ground its AI offering in operational reality, where context, coordination and control matter as much as speed, according to Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Certinia’s recent announcement of Veda is more profound than it may appear on the surface,” he said. “Veda is notable not simply because it introduces a new suite of AI agents and intelligent workflow-based actions, but because it offers a glimpse into what the future of enterprise AI is likely to look like: AI that works alongside humans in consequential workflows, helps people make better decisions and earns trust by being grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.”

Since the launch of Veda in April, Certinia has taken several actions to enhance its AI capabilities. In July, the firm acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform purpose-built for the professional services sector.

This acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can now connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review, according to Hebner.

“Certinia provides the deep, structured foundation of professional services, customer success and financial management; Moonnox brings the missing half: capturing the unstructured reality — the emails, chats, and calls — where delivery actually happens,” he explained. “Together, they fuse everything a services business knows with everything their teams do, moving Veda beyond orchestration toward context-aware, AI-native services delivery.”

The context graph can also draw on structured records such as timecard entries and utilization figures. Moonnox helps bring that information into the graph for client-facing teams managing projects, according to Cesafsky.

“That’s been where Moonnox has really showed up for us over the last couple of months,” he said. “It’s those capabilities to help the client-facing services [and] delivery teams run and operate their projects. [Moonnox] is effectively an intake machine for a lot of that structured data to bring that into the context graph as well.”

In September, Certinia unveiled its System of Action for services businesses. The offering significantly expanded the Veda AI suite with new agents and more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135.

Certinia’s System of Action uses a three-tier architecture to bring AI agents into services workflows. The first tier brings together structured records and unstructured project data. The second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia’s experience in services to inform decisions. The third lets agents act within existing workflows.

“We want to accelerate the delivery for our customers,” Malhotra said. “Our customers are solving some specific problems in the professional services world. We don’t want to just give you a project plan. If you choose to execute that project plan with some agents, we’ll give you that. If you want to really think about agentic capabilities to help you in making money, in expanding your time [and] in terms of delivery, we will help you with that.”

For professional services firms, adopting AI agents means deciding which parts of project delivery to delegate to them.

“We view professional services as a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability,” Hebner said. “If Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes.”

#5654. NYC Votes To Cut Construction Red Tape in Bid To Spur More Homebuilding

New York City voters overwhelmingly approved a plan to overhaul the city's notoriously complicated construction permitting process on Tuesday, handing Mayor Zohran Mamdani a victory in his effort to accelerate housing development.

Question 4, 1 of 5 ballot measures approved in the Nov. 3 election, received roughly 68% support, according to preliminary election results.

The measure promises to simplify construction by bringing 40 types of permits and approvals currently handled by 18 separate government offices and agencies into one centralized digital system.

"New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do," Mamdani said in a statement on Tuesday night. The reforms would "directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love."

However, the new system isn't required to launch until 2030. Even when it does, faster permitting will address only one of the many obstacles making housing so difficult and expensive to build in New York.

"No single reform will be a silver bullet for housing supply and affordability, especially in a city like New York," explains Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Instead, each pro-supply policy change is a baby step in the right direction. And these marginal gains will add up."

The Big Apple needs approximately 700,000 additional homes over the next decade to meet existing and future demand, according to an August 2026 draft assessment from the city's housing and planning departments.

Yet developers filed plans for just 8,064 multifamily units in the second quarter of 2026, in a stunning 52% decline from the previous quarter, according to the Real Estate Board of New York.

That amounts to less than half the 17,500 new homes the city needs to add each quarter—and they're only proposed units, not completed homes.

Centralizing permits could help close that gap by cutting down the time and cost builders are forced to spend navigating city bureaucracy.

"Streamlining approvals can make a huge difference," Krimmel says. "It might not be the flashiest reform, but when it comes to new construction, time is money."

And permitting takes a very, very long time in New York City.

Of the nearly five years it takes to build a typical 20-unit apartment building in the Big Apple, roughly 1.5 years are spent securing permits alone, according to a September 2026 study examining construction timelines across 60 U.S. cities.

Now compare that to similar projects in Raleigh, NC, or Phoenix, where it takes roughly two years from application to completion.

"In a city like New York City with high land acquisition costs and a complex regulatory environment, predictability in timelines and financing can be critical for ensuring new construction can pencil," Krimmel says.

Research suggests those time savings could translate into more homes.

Cutting approval times by 25% could have increased multifamily housing production in Los Angeles by 12.7% between 2010 and 2022, according to a 2026 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics.

When researchers accounted for additional development that faster approvals might encourage, the estimated increase reached 23.7%.

The question for New Yorkers, though, is when those reforms might translate into more housing options and lower rents. The median monthly asking rent hit $3,785 in October—up 4.5% from a year ago.

Under the new rules, applicants would have one digital portal to submit documents, track applications, and obtain approvals, rather than navigating separate systems across multiple agencies.

But streamlining applications doesn't necessarily mean they'll be reviewed any faster.

In fact, the average time required to approve applications through the Department of Buildings' existing digital portal climbed from 8.3 days in 2020 to 20.3 days in 2025, according to a July report from New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli.

And its hardly the only challenge. Krimmel says the overhaul won't address other barriers to construction, including zoning restrictions and the complexity of financing multifamily developments.

Still, he sees the reform as one step toward untangling a much larger problem.

"In the same way that a complex web of red tape and veto points is extremely good at creating barriers to new construction, real solutions will require the city untangles that web bit by bit," he says.

With the new system potentially four years away, the first test will be whether it actually shortens permitting timelines. Any corresponding increase in housing construction—and relief for renters—could take considerably longer.

As Mamdani acknowledged on Tuesday night, "Now comes the work of turning these votes into results."

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5653. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. Finding the right one could be as simple as getting more information about tools like ARMs. A trusted lender can run the numbers with you, walk you through the what-ifs, and help you explore the possibilities.Is an ARM a good option for you? Talk to a loan officer to find out.

#5652. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. #5651. NEAR Protocol Tokenomics Overhaul Catapults The Crypto Coin 10% Higher

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

NEAR Protocol is climbing as the market weighs a major tokenomics overhaul designed to reduce token inflation and ease long-term selling pressure. The NEAR rally follows crypto governance approval of a proposal to lower the network’s annual issuance ceiling from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years.

The proposal, known as HSP-029, passed with overwhelming support from NEAR’s House of Stake. It would gradually reduce the number of new tokens entering circulation, potentially strengthening the supply outlook as the network expands.

NEAR Plans to Take Millions of Tokens Out of Future IssuanceNEAR Protocol's (@NEARProtocol) $NEAR House of Stake has approved a proposal to reduce maximum annual token issuance from 2.5% to 1.6%.The change will roll out gradually over 24 months, reducing the issuance ceiling… pic.twitter.com/pmPOUrWhoI

The move comes as NEAR Protocol seeks to turn its growing ecosystem activity into stronger value for token holders. With issuance cuts, cross-chain infrastructure, and renewed trading interest converging, we are watching if NEAR can sustain its latest breakout.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The approved proposal would reduce NEAR’s maximum annual issuance rate from 2.5% to 1.6%, with the change phased in over 24 months. According to the proposal, the reduction could prevent 11.8 million NEAR from entering circulation during the first two years. Over six years, the avoided issuance could reach 66.1 million tokens.

At full implementation, daily issuance would fall from roughly 89,500 NEAR to 57,300 NEAR. The network would retain its existing distribution of newly issued tokens, with 90% going to staking participants and 10% allocated to the protocol treasury.

The overhaul also introduces a trade-off for stakers. Gross staking yields could decline from approximately 5.27% to 3.37%, assuming staking participation remains unchanged.

However, the proposal still requires Security Council review, a 90-day grace period, and validator adoption before the changes become binding.

Beyond tokenomics, NEAR Protocol continues developing its chain-signature technology, which allows accounts to interact with external blockchains. NEAR Intents also supports cross-chain swaps, giving the ecosystem another potential source of activity and fee revenue.

The combination of lower issuance and expanding utility is giving NEAR crypto bulls a fresh narrative. However, the market will need to see sustained demand before the supply reduction translates into a lasting price trend.

NEAR Protocol’s cross-chain ambitions arrive as Bitcoin infrastructure projects compete to bring more functionality to the world’s largest cryptocurrency.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning itself as a Bitcoin Layer-2 network designed to support faster transactions, lower fees, and smart-contract functionality. Its architecture aims to connect Bitcoin’s security and liquidity with applications typically associated with more flexible blockchain ecosystems.

Bitcoin Hyper has begun rolling out testnet infrastructure, including a wallet and explorer, as it prepares for broader network testing.

Did somebody order a little extra Bitcoin utility? 👀⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4FWNQ pic.twitter.com/bQAMiOcdUD

While NEAR Protocol is building cross-chain functionality across multiple networks, Bitcoin Hyper is focusing directly on expanding Bitcoin’s role in decentralized finance. This could become important if Bitcoin holders increasingly seek access to applications, trading, and other on-chain opportunities without moving away from BTC-focused infrastructure.

The project is approaching its planned November 26, 2026, launch, with its presale entering the final stretch. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.2 million, while HYPER is priced at just $0.0136.

The project also offers staking rewards of 35% APY, adding another incentive for early participants ahead of its anticipated token launch.

With the presale scheduled to end on November 26, the approaching launch is becoming a key milestone for HYPER holders watching for exchange listings and ecosystem growth.

NEAR crypto is trading around the $3.80 area, leaving the $4 level as an important near-term hurdle. A sustained move above $4 could strengthen the recovery narrative and open the door toward the $4.30 region. A stronger breakout could bring the $4.50 area into focus, particularly if broader altcoin sentiment improves.

The tokenomics overhaul gives bulls a fundamental catalyst, but traders will also need to see stronger spot demand and improving market momentum.

On the downside, a failure to hold the $3.70–$3.80 area could expose NEAR to another test of support near $3.50. Continued weakness across the broader crypto market would make a sustained recovery more difficult.

For now, NEAR Protocol has a clear catalyst in its issuance reduction proposal, alongside continued development of its cross-chain ecosystem. The next stage of the crypto rally depends on whether buyers can turn the tokenomics story into sustained demand and push NEAR beyond its immediate resistance levels.

#5650. North Carolina Passes New Limits on Property Tax Levies

On Tuesday, North Carolina voters narrowly approved House Bill 1089, which proposed a limit on property tax increases. The amendment needed 60% of voters to support it to pass. It received 60.4% support.

The amendment does not specify the terms of those limits. Instead, that will be up to the North Carolina General Assembly to decide.

Proponents, including North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, contended that surging property assessments have enabled local governments to impose excessive tax burdens on residents without delivering proportional public services.

Last year, Hall formed the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform, a 23-member committee to examine property taxes in the state.

“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” Hall said in a press release earlier this year.

Support for the amendment fell across party lines. Conservatives and commercial organizations supported the measure, arguing that the amendment would help curb local government spending and protect property owners.

Political pundits theorized that the ballot measures were meant to entice Republican voters to the polls during an off-election year. But Western Carolina University professor Chris Cooper told NPR's All Things Considered the theory didn't hold much weight.

"The notion that North Carolinians were not going to show up and vote from the Republican persuasion, but now they are because of a constitutional amendment, is on there, frankly that stretches credibility for me a little bit."

But critics of the proposal said that creating a property tax cap would hobble local governments. Furthermore, the North Carolina Housing Coalition argued that the proposal would most benefit larger corporate property owners while providing little benefit to owners of single-family homes.

Tamika Walker Kelly, president of the North Carolina Association of Educators, criticized the bill for favoring “tax breaks over classrooms.”

“When local revenue is constrained, schools feel it immediately with overcrowded classrooms, aging school buildings, and educators stretched too thin,” Walker Kelly told NC Newsline. “A constitutional cap does not protect struggling families. It protects the largest landowners in the state, while the families who depend on public schools are left with less.”

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in North Carolina is 0.66%, which is relatively low compared with states such as New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5649. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5648. Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor, whose app runs several coding agents at once

Meta Platforms Inc. has acquired artificial intelligence coding startup Conductor in a deal first reported today by Axios.

Conductor confirmed it’s joining Meta in a post on its website. Terms were not disclosed.

The company’s software lets a developer run several coding agents at once, each in an isolated copy of the codebase, and then review and merge what they produce. Supported agents include Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s Cursor, and users pay for them through their own subscriptions and keys.

The desktop app runs on Macs. A hosted version, Conductor Cloud, puts agents in sandboxed virtual machines where they can keep working for hours, and users can check on them from an iPhone app.

Engineers at Meta were using Conductor well before the deal. When the startup announced its Series A in March, it named Meta, Google LLC and Spotify Technology SA among the companies with dozens of engineers on the product. Conductor now says on its website that more than 100,000 people use it.

People familiar with the deal told Axios that Meta expects the Conductor team’s speed at shipping products to help it build its next generation of AI coding tools. The acquisition follows two Meta model releases last month that both pitched coding as a strength.

On Oct. 15, Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weights version of its Muse Spark model aimed at coding and long-running agent work. Meta’s more capable Muse Wonder models stay closed inside its own Muse Code terminal and application programming interface.

The Conductor deal landed the same day OpenAI said it plans to acquire developer tools startup Pierre Computer. OpenAI had already announced plans in June to buy Ona, which runs coding agents in cloud sandboxes.

Local copies of the Mac app keep working until early 2027, when the team expects to release a new interface it has not yet described. New models and critical bug fixes stop arriving at that point, and Conductor will delete the app’s user data. The company said it has never sold Conductor user data or trained models on it, and does not plan to.

Chief Executive Charlie Holtz and Chief Technology Officer Jackson de Campos founded the company, formally Melty Inc., in 2024. Conductor raised a $22 million Series A in March from Spark Capital and Matrix. Y Combinator and the founders of Notion and Linear are also backers.

#5646. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5645. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5644. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5643. A $6.52 Million Beverlywood Home on a Lavish Golf Course Just Set the Record for the Priciest Teardown Sale

A Los Angeles property in Beverlywood has been sold in an off-market transaction, and at $6.52 million, it has set the record for the most expensive home to be purchased with plans to be torn down in the upscale neighborhood.

The dwelling is certainly in a coveted location, perched directly on the Hillcrest Country Club—a private club with an 18-hole golf course that has attracted celebrity members for more than a century.

According to Town and Country Magazine, the club’s initiation fee is a reported $185,000. Comedian Adam Sandler, singer-songwriter Neil Diamond, and Paramount co-founder Adolph Zukor are among the Hillcrest’s most notable members.

The home currently standing at 1807 Roxbury Drive is a three-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom abode spanning 2,874 square feet. It was built in 1953.

According to Micah Hiller of Prime Rock Realty, who represented the seller and buyer of 1807 Roxbury Drive, the new residents are looking to build a new house with a luxury construction company called Drexel Luxury Homes. They’d like a home with a much larger footprint.

The lot itself is 8,660 square feet, and Hiller estimates the buyers will be able to build a home that’s “at least” 4,500 square feet without a basement. Should they decide to add a lower ground floor, they’d likely be able to add an additional 2,000 or 3,000 square feet.

“This is the highest land-value sale in Beverlywood’s history,” Hiller tells Realtor.com®.

Hiller explains that Beverlywood has become a highly sought-after enclave, which, “despite the current market, continues to show incredible strength.”

“From what I’m seeing, demand for the neighborhood has only grown, and in some ways, it has become even more desirable than Beverly Hills,” he continues. “Buyers appreciate the community, location, and opportunity to create a home here.”

Beverlywood has seen some year-over-year softness in the housing market with the median listing price, price per square foot, and median days on the market all showing decreases from this time last year, according to Realtor.com data.

Still, each of these metrics is outperforming nationwide stats. In Beverlywood, the average listing is just under $2.4 million, while that number is just under $420,000 for the country as a whole.

Homes here also spend less than half the time on the market than they do nationwide, with Beverlywood listings being snapped up in an average of 29 days. The U.S. median is 61.

For the Los Angeles neighborhood, this number is down 21.62% year over year, signaling faster turnover and a more competitive environment for sellers.

As of October 2026, Beverlywood had an impressive sale-to-list price ratio of 99%, indicating a strong seller’s market for this desirable spot. There are also fewer opportunities for a buyer to find exactly what they’re looking for, as there are only a dozen active listings for sale.

Beverlywood is not the only corner of the country with a competitive market setting records.

In Provincetown, MA—where the price per square foot is six times the national median—the record for most-expensive condo sold was broken twice in a two-week period.

Thomas Andrews of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty, who was the listing agent on both pricey transactions, said the vibrant community is the reason the local market is so coveted—which is quite similar to what Hiller says of Beverlywood.

“Provincetown is such a magical place. You have your Martha’s Vineyard, you have your Nantucket, but there’s so much soul in the creative arts in Provincetown that just makes it super vibrant and super sought-after,” he said.

Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones explains that the town has effectively reached its limit for new housing, which creates a tense battle for anyone who wants to find a home there.

"Provincetown sits at the very tip of Cape Cod, which means there is essentially no more space to build," she explains. "The housing stock is therefore relatively fixed, and any new supply has to come off from redevelopment or small-scale infill, both of which tend to be expensive and difficult to pull off."

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5642. Cyber ups and downs: Datadog falls 14% on outlook tied to one customer as Rapid7 jumps and Fastly slides

Datadog Inc., Rapid7 Inc. and Fastly Inc. all beat Wall Street’s third-quarter forecasts today, but Rapid7 was the only one of the three to see its shares rise.

A cautious outlook tied to one large customer knocked about 14% off Datadog’s stock in regular trading. Rapid7 jumped 18% after hours on results that came despite a decline in revenue.

For its third quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Datadog reported adjusted earnings of 81 cents per share, up from 55 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 64 cents per share on revenue of $1.14 billion.

Unadjusted net income climbed to $118.3 million from $33.9 million, and the adjusted operating margin widened five points to 28%. Billings in the quarter rose 30% to $1.16 billion, Chief Financial Officer David Obstler said on the earnings call, with remaining performance obligations up 38% at $3.85 billion. Free cash flow came to $251 million.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Olivier Pomel told analysts that more than 850 artificial intelligence companies now use Datadog, roughly 100 more than at the end of June. Adoption is strong across the platform as customers scale “their digital operations and use of AI,” he said in the earnings release. Customers worth $100,000 or more a year in recurring revenue rose 20% to about 4,860.

Full-year guidance went up. Datadog now expects 2026 revenue of $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion, against the $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion it projected in August, and adjusted earnings of $2.73 to $2.75 per share. Fourth-quarter adjusted earnings are forecast at 69 to 71 cents per share.

Revenue for the fourth quarter is guided at $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly what analysts had expected, with the top of the range only about $3 million above third-quarter revenue. The forecast assumes Datadog’s largest customer, an AI provider the company has not named, spends no more than its contractual minimum, according to Obstler.

Usage on that account dropped in the third quarter while staying above the floor. Excluding it, implied fourth-quarter growth is in the low- to mid-30% range. Early renewals with some large AI customers, signed at higher commitments in return for better pricing, are also holding back near-term revenue.

The roughly 14% drop today made it two straight quarters in which a beat failed to hold up the stock. Datadog shares closed 19% lower in August, the day the company disclosed the customer’s planned cutback.

In Rapid7’s third quarter, also ended Sept. 30, the cybersecurity company posted adjusted earnings of 60 cents per share, up from 57 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $212.4 million, down 2.5% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 46 cents per share on revenue of $209 million.

Annualized recurring revenue slipped 2.2%, to $819.7 million, ahead of the roughly $812 million the company had guided to in August. Adjusted operating income rose to $46.2 million from $36.9 million. Unadjusted net income fell to $3.5 million from $9.8 million after $10 million in restructuring costs from the 12% workforce cut announced in August and a $5.5 million write-down on a strategic equity investment.

Rapid7 demonstrated its Agentic SOC at Black Hat USA in August, using AI agents to speed up investigations while leaving high-impact decisions to analysts. Wael Mohamed, who took over as CEO in June, said the core business “is becoming more stable” and that “one quarter of stability is just a start.” Rapid7 is “not declaring victory,” he added.

The company’s full-year adjusted earnings forecast moved to $1.94 to $1.96 per share, well above the $1.78 to $1.83 it gave three months ago. Revenue guidance edged up to $841 million to $843 million. For the fourth quarter, Rapid7 sees revenue of $208 million to $210 million, down 3% to 4% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of 53 to 55 cents per share.

The stock climbed about 18% in extended trading.

Edge cloud platform provider Fastly reported adjusted earnings of 17 cents per share for its third quarter, up from 7 cents a year earlier, on record revenue of $190.2 million, up 20% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 12 cents per share on revenue of $187.9 million.

Most of Fastly’s revenue still comes from network services, which grew 16%, to $138 million. Security sales rose twice as fast, to $44.7 million, in a quarter when the company also launched AI Firewall to block prompt injection and other attacks before they reach a model. Trailing-12-month net retention was its highest since 2022, at 119%. The top 10 customers now account for 39% of revenue, up from 32% a year ago.

Fourth-quarter revenue is forecast at $198 million to $202 million, ahead of the $197 million analysts had modeled. Full-year revenue guidance moved up to $744 million to $748 million from $732 million to $746 million in August. Adjusted earnings for 2026 are now expected at 61 to 63 cents per share. None of that stopped Fastly shares from falling about 14% after the bell.
