#5641. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5640. Homebuilder Stocks Surge as Democratic Sweep Raises Hopes for Affordability Gains

Homebuilders and housing suppliers saw significant jumps in their share prices following the stunning success of Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

At the closing bell on Wednesday, shares of major builders Lennar and PulteGroup were up more than 7% on the day, and D.R. Horton rose more than 8%.

Suppliers showed similar increases. Home Depot finished the day up 6.5%, after spiking as much as 17% during midday trading, according to Yahoo Finance. Lowe’s Companies ended the day up 7.5%, but also had a midday spike to 15% before giving back some gains.

For comparison, the broad S&P 500 index ended the day up 1.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3%, or more than 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since April 2025.

The stock market surge comes in the wake of Tuesday’s midterm election, where Democrats gained control of Congress in a dramatic sweep.

The homebuilding sector has faced massive cost increases in recent years. Several factors have played into the building sector’s hardships, which have led to a shortfall of roughly 4 million homes throughout the U.S., according to a March report from Realtor.com®.

Tariffs, supply chain issues, and inflation have caused substantial increases in material costs, according to Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial Group.

“Labor continues to be a major issue, with a shortage of skilled workers driving wages higher,” Gestiehr tells Realtor.com. “Add in land prices, permitting, insurance, and financing costs, and it becomes increasingly difficult to build homes at prices the average buyer can afford.”

Builders have experienced a squeeze from both sides, Gestiehr explains, because at the same time that the cost to build a home has increased, skyrocketing mortgage rates have put limits on what buyers can afford.

Just days ago, major builders including D.R. Horton and the PulteGroup reported net income declines, with PulteGroup CEO Ryan Marshall stating that the company’s year-over-year net income dropped by 17% in the third quarter.

Suddenly, there’s a renewed sense of optimism surrounding the industry after Tuesday’s election results.

While the underlying challenges remain, Gestiehr says that investors are likely expecting more federal attention to turn to policies surrounding affordability.

“Housing affordability has become a major concern, and investors may be anticipating more attention on policies that encourage new construction and make homeownership more affordable,” says Gestiehr. “Investors may be anticipating additional housing incentives, policies that encourage new construction, and potentially lower mortgage rates.”

Affordability, particularly when it comes to housing, was a key part of many Democratic candidate platforms.

To address affordability overall, there should be focus on building up the supply of homes before offering incentives for buyers and spurring more demand, says Gestiehr.

"If you increase demand without increasing supply, you may end up pushing home prices even higher,” adds Gestiehr. “Reducing regulatory costs, streamlining permitting, encouraging additional development, and potentially lowering tariffs on building materials could all help builders.”

Rolling back tariffs was a major talking point for several incoming Democrat senators, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Texas’ James Talarico, as well as Alaska’s Mary Peltola, whose race results were pending.

Gestiehr maintains that many other factors, including inflation, interest rates, employment, and corporate earnings, as well as actual policy changes, will still have a much greater impact on homebuilder results than the election results alone. It’s not uncommon for markets to perform well following midterm elections, in part because the uncertainty surrounding the election is removed.

“The election may have given homebuilders a reason to be optimistic, but optimism doesn't necessarily translate into stronger earnings,” says Gestiehr. “At some point, these companies need to see improvement in demand, affordability, and profit margins to justify higher stock prices.”

Congress already passed one major bipartisan housing bill this year, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. The bill lays out 45 provisions aimed at cutting red tape and constructing more homes, as well as banning institutional investor homebuyers.

Adding new members to Congress, many of whom have been elected on the promise of ushering in affordability, could mean more meaningful change is on the way.

“With a divided government, I wouldn’t expect major changes overnight, but housing affordability is an area where both parties have an incentive to find common ground,” says Gestiehr.

#5639. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. #5638. Block DOJ Settlement: Jack Dorsey’s Company Faces $764M Deal as Bitcoin Profit Plunges 50%

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Block DOJ settlement talks have reached a major turning point, with Jack Dorsey-owned payments company agreeing in principle to pay $764 million. The proposed deal would resolve a federal investigation into alleged failures in its anti-money laundering controls.

The agreement follows years of scrutiny over Block’s Cash App compliance practices. The company disclosed the development in its quarterly filing yesterday, outlining a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice.

Jack Dorsey’s Block has beaten Q3 earnings estimates, posting $3.2B in gross profit.The company has also raised its 2026 outlook, while warning that a potential DOJ settlement could be larger than expected.Strong results and a higher forecast from one of the biggest names in… pic.twitter.com/Bk0KByUDPV

The announcement arrives alongside a sharp decline in Block’s Bitcoin business. Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit plunged 50% year-over-year to $52 million during the third quarter, despite stronger overall company earnings.

The proposed Block DOJ agreement would defer prosecution for three years over allegations that the company failed to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. The DOJ’s investigation centers on compliance requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act. Block would need to meet obligations outlined in the agreement throughout its term.

If the company fully complies, prosecutors would move to dismiss the deferred charges. However, the resolution remains subject to final agreement terms and court approval.

The proposed settlement carries a gross monetary component of approximately $964 million. Credits for previous regulatory resolutions would reduce the expected net payment to roughly $764 million. Block has already accrued $764 million for the matter as of September 30. The company warned that the final cost could exceed that amount.

The investigation dates back to 2023, when federal authorities began examining Block’s compliance practices and related disclosures. The scrutiny followed allegations raised by short seller Hindenburg Research.

Block rejected those allegations as inaccurate and misleading. Separately, New York’s financial regulator fined the company $40 million in 2025 over compliance failures.

The Block DOJ development comes as the company’s Bitcoin business faces a sharp profitability decline. Block reported Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit of $52 million in Q3, down from $104 million a year earlier. The company attributed the decline primarily to lower fees on certain Bitcoin transactions through Cash App.

Bitcoin-related revenue reached approximately $1.8 billion during the quarter. However, the lower fees significantly reduced the amount Block retained from its Bitcoin operations.

The weakness contrasts with stronger performance across the broader business. Block reported $3.24 billion in total gross profit, up 22% year-over-year. Cash App gross profit climbed 27% to $2.07 billion. Square gross profit increased 14%, while quarterly net income rose to approximately $566 million.

Block also raised its full-year 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, representing expected growth of roughly 22%.

Now, proposed Block DOJ settlement creates a major legal expense alongside a mixed earnings picture. Its Bitcoin business is generating less profit, even as Cash App and Square support stronger company-wide growth.

#5637. Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep

Shares of Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. closed higher today following Democrats’ resounding midterm victory.

Amazon jumped 8.3% at one point and ended the trading session 6.1% higher than Tuesday. Microsoft gained nearly 6.7% while Alphabet and Google rose by about 3.1% and 1.4%, respectively. Multiple industry analysts tied the stock gains to the companies’ artificial intelligence buildout.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on a campaign that emphasized data center restrictions. Furthermore, voters approved 40 ballot measures focused on blocking or limiting AI infrastructure projects. Bloomberg cited Robert Pavlik, a senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, as saying that tech giants’ shares jumped because investors believe a data center slowdown could improve their finances.

Amazon, Meta and Google have become cash-flow-negative in recent months because of their steep infrastructure investments. Last Wednesday, the search giant reported a negative cash flow that exceeded the consensus estimate by about $6.4 billion. Google’s stock price plummeted 10% in after-hours trading even though its cloud revenue more than doubled.

Needham & Co., B. ‌Riley ⁠Wealth and prominent tech industry analyst Ben Thompson highlighted another possible contributor to the stock rally. New restrictions on AI projects would make computing infrastructure more scarce, which would boost the value of existing data centers. That would benefit the tech giants that logged share price gains today.

Thompson noted that neoclouds, or emerging AI-focused cloud providers, may also benefit in certain respects. Developments for which they have already secured regulatory permission could become more valuable. At the same time, they may find it more difficult to finance new sites.

That dynamic weighed on chip stocks today. Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. both shed more than 3% of their value, while Broadcom Inc. declined 2%. SK hynix Inc., the world’s largest supplier of HBM memory for graphics cards, dropped by more than 5%. One notable exception was Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which ended the trading day about 1% higher.

Thompson noted that the midterms could also affect the AI industry in other ways. He pointed out that a stricter regulatory environment may give space-based data centers a boost. Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, in turn, could see their hardware costs decline if new restrictions are placed on frontier model training. Such a development may ease their path to profitability.

Last month, Meta announced plans to sell up to $95 billion in shares to finance new data centers. On Monday, Oracle Corp. filed to issue $20 billion worth of bonds and shares in connection with its own AI buildout. It’s currently unclear how the midterm results will affect those initiatives and other large-scale data center projects currently underway.

#5636. Inside the $8.9 Million Dallas Treehouse Estate Modeled After a Nautilus Shell, Complete With a Natatorium

A Preston Hollow estate modeled after a nautilus shell is back on the market in Dallas—this time asking $8,875,000.

The property at 5110 Park Lane has been on and off the market since May, when it debuted at $9,999,000.

The residence, a "limestone-and-copper nautilus" by architect Michael Murphy, totals more than 17,000 square feet across the 14,921-square-foot main house and a 2,378-square-foot attached natatorium. The estate is represented by Faisal Halum of Compass RE Texas.

Even in a neighborhood as prestigious as Preston Hollow, where residents have included former President George W. Bush and Mark Cuban, the design of the estate is anything but conventional. Wedge-shaped rooms fan outward from a central elevator, an arrangement meant to give every room a view. With the house set among mature trees, the effect is something like living in a treehouse, suspended in the canopy.

The 1.67-acre lot features rolling terrain, dense foliage, and a creek that winds through the grounds. Warm-toned Lueders limestone, quarried in Texas specifically for the project, carries from the exterior into the interiors, blurring the line between the two.

The primary living quarters occupy the upper level, where buffed concrete floors and Venetian plaster walls are paired with more limestone. Three bedrooms are in the main residence, and a separate guest apartment adds two more. There are five full bathrooms and four half-baths.

The lower level was built for both work and play. It holds office space, media rooms, conference areas, and a workout room, along with the natatorium—where a lap pool features a waterfall lit by fiber optics. The grounds are enclosed by a gated wrought-iron fence, and there is parking for five vehicles.

The property is located close to the shops and restaurants of Highland Park Village and Inwood Village, as well as some of the city’s top private schools.

Dallas Love Field is also nearby, making the home convenient for part-time residents or frequent travelers.

#5635. Zillow Says Lawsuits in the Past, ‘Not Obvious’ How Market Recovers

Real estate’s biggest name is struggling, just like everyone else, but company leadership is promising that it—and the industry—have ways to hang on amid a tech revolution, a sluggish market and legal woes the company claims are in the past now.

Speaking to investors after reporting earnings for Q3 2026, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business,” with CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann adding that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

Zillow’s report comes as mortgage rates remain elevated from earlier this year and existing home sales are on track to come in around 4 million—down more than 20% from pre-pandemic norms. The company’s stock fell sharply, down around 17% in after-hours trading.

The company still faces a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Democratic lawmakers previously offered pointed criticism of some of Zillow’s business practices, which are also used by at least some other portals, as the party made big gains in the midterms yesterday.

On the tech side, Zillow said it has not seen major impacts from increased use of AI by consumers, or Google’s ongoing push into residential real estate.

“(Google’s program) is very different than a ‘Preferred’ connection and an integrated transaction and helping agents grow their business that way. So we haven’t seen any impact from it today, even though it’s supposedly live nationwide,” Wacksman said.

As the company previously announced, agent partners are all being transitioned from other programs to the company’s Zillow Preferred service, which executives said is integrated with Zillow Home Loans.

The transition is expected to be fully implemented by the first half of 2027, and 75% complete by the end of this year.

Zillow’s residential for-sale revenue was down 4% year-over-year, $419 million in Q3 2026 compared to $435 million in Q3 2025. On the other hand, mortgage revenue grew 32%, and the company touted durable rental income, up 26% from the same period last year.

Overall revenue came in up 7% from last year at $724 million, with the lawsuit payment—$165 million after insurance covered part of the settlement—dinging the top—line. Outlook for Q4—historically the slowest for real estate—was $635 to $665 million, roughly the same as last year’s reported $654 million.

Late last year, Zillow was targeted by a high-profile class-action firm with claims from recent homebuyers focused on those “lead diversion” and loan referral practices. A judge initially threw that lawsuit out (though plaintiffs are seeking to revive it).

The company also agreed last week to pay $212.5 million to settle a lawsuit over its long-shuttered iBuying business, something the company said it was happy to put behind it.

“I think we’ve been pretty consistent and transparent to the degree we could be, that we didn’t expect these cases to impact business. And I think as you’re seeing them resolve, get settled, move on, you’re seeing that come to light. They’re not impacting our business,” Wacksman said.

As far as the macro picture, Hofmann said that without any sign of a market rebound, “its our job (to) just keep driving on the underlying structural growth drivers we have,” including software and rentals that are not rate dependent.

“We’re also fortunate in that the business has diversified pretty rapidly over the last four or five years,” he said.

Addressing the use of agentic AI and potential changes in how consumers search for homes, Wacksman and Hofmann both promised that Zillow’s model was built to thrive in this new environment.

“We see the human experiences remaining human,” Wacksman said. “The dreaming and shopping part is the part you want to do and the transaction part is the part you need to do, and Zillow is the best place to do both those things…and then our ability to make the professional’s job easier so they can serve the customer better is where we’re focused, and why we are so confident in the strategy.”

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5634. The chips are down: Qualcomm falls on revenue miss, weak guidance; Arm and GlobalFoundries do little better

Chipmakers Qualcomm Inc., Arm Holdings Ltd. and GlobalFoundries Ltd. struggled to move the needle today after reporting financial results that clearly left investors wanting more.

After an impressive earnings beat from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. just 24 hours earlier, investors may have had heightened expectations. But if they did, on a day when the market rocketed higher on the U.S. election results, they were clearly let down by the shaky performance of Qualcomm, which beat expectations on earnings but missed on revenue and offered weak guidance. The result was predictable, with its stock down more than 6% after-hours.

Both Arm and GlobalFoundries did better, but it wasn’t enough to satisfy investors who are becoming increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence industry that has driven significant growth for all three chipmakers over the last couple of years.

The biggest disappointment was Qualcomm, which reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.17 per share on revenue of $10.44 billion, up just 8% from a year earlier. The results were mixed, with Wall Street looking for earnings of $2.16 per share on sales of $10.48 billion. For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it’s looking for earnings of around $2.25 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range on sales of $10.48 billion, falling short of the Street’s target of $2.27 per share in earnings and $10.48 billion in revenue.

Qualcomm’s troubles stem from the fact that it has less exposure to the AI industry’s rampant growth than many other chipmakers. The bulk of its sales comes from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. But the market is currently reeling due to the rising cost of components such as memory, which have forced handset makers to bump up their prices, reducing demand. Qualcomm has tried to weather the storm by raising the prices of its own chips recently, but its smartphone chip sales fell 26% in the quarter to just $5.14 billion, well behind the Street’s target of $5.21 billion.

Under Chief Executive Cristiano Amon (pictured), Qualcomm has tried to pivot and grow its position in alternative chip markets, particularly the AI data center industry. Revenue from that segment rose to $650 million during the quarter, but it’s still dwarfed by the smartphone business.

Nonetheless, Amon insisted that the company will grow its data center business to more than $5 billion in revenue by the end of fiscal 2027. He said the company recently struck a deal with an unnamed global hyperscaler for optical connectivity chips. “We don’t have a demand issue; it’s a supply issue,” he told analysts on a conference call. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better.”

Qualcomm’s automotive business was a bright spot, with sales there rising 89% to $1.99 billion in the quarter, above the Street’s consensus estimate of $1.66 billion. Internet of Things revenue came to $1.88 billion, up 4% from a year ago and just ahead of the Street’s estimate.

Finally, there’s Qualcomm’s QTL business, which generates revenue from licensing intellectual property for modems, 5G connectivity and other technologies. That segment added $1.3 billion in revenue, down 7%, despite signing renewed licensing agreements with Apple Inc., Transsion Inc. and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd.

Chip design company Arm delivered much more palatable results, but it was somewhat cautious with its guidance for the current quarter, and its stock was down 2% in late trading today. The company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, just beating the Street’s target of 48 cents, while revenue rose 27% from a year earlier, to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion analyst estimate.

Unlike Qualcomm, Arm doesn’t manufacture complete chips for its customers, but instead designs and licenses processor blueprints for customers such as Apple Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Qualcomm to build their own custom chips. Where Arm is more similar to Qualcomm is in its strategy, where it too is also pivoting to focus on data center chip designs, trying to tap into the demand for AI compute. Arm said its data center business was the main growth driver this year, with royalties there doubling year-over-year.

However, Arm’s guidance did little to excite investors. The company said it’s looking for earnings of 56 cents per share, plus or minus four cents, compared with Wall Street’s forecast of 55 cents per share. For revenue, it’s targeting $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, which is just ahead of the Street’s $1.52 billion target.

GlobalFoundries did a little better than its peers today, posting results and guidance for the current that squeaked past expectations. However, its stock remained flat after-hours.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on sales of $1.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, with growth driven by strong demand from AI and data center customers, it said. The results were better than expected, with analysts targeting earnings of 51 cents on revenue of $1.89 billion.

GlobalFoundries’ also differs from Qualcomm, in that it’s a pure-play contract manufacturer that builds the processors designed by semiconductors firms, rather than designing chips itself or selling them under its own brand. Qualcomm is actually one of its biggest customers, alongside Broadcom Inc., NXP Semiconductors N.V. and Infineon Technologies Inc. As such, its fortunes are very much aligned with those of the chip designers it caters too.

For the current quarter, GlobalFoundries said it’s looking for earnings of 59 cents per share, plus or minus five cents, on revenue of about $2 billion. Wall Street is looking for earnings of 57 cents per share and has the same revenue target.

#5633. Inside ‘My Big Fat Fabulous Life’ Star Whitney Way Thore’s ‘Dopamine Apartment’

When “My Big Fat Fabulous Life” star Whitney Way Thore moved back to her home state of North Carolina, she fell in love with Jake Beaudoin—and the whimsical Charlotte apartment they now share.

The 42-year-old reality TV personality began renting the “tiny, but enough” one-bedroom, one-bathroom, 830-square-foot unit in December 2025 following her unintentionally brief residency at a New England-style cottage in Salem, MA.

“I love Salem so much, but I had some issues that we didn't really cover in the season, some extended family things. My dad needed a little bit more help at home, so I decided to come on back,” Thore reveals in the latest installment of Celebrity Sanctuary.

Rather than returning to her old stomping ground at the Greensboro, NC, home she still holds or her family’s nearby property, Thore settled into a place inside a “new and modern” building where she could focus on a fresh start with her dog Goosie, cat Wandaleezza Rice, and shortly after her arrival, Beaudoin, now her fiancé.

In an exclusive clip shared with Realtor.com® from the Season 14 premiere of Thore’s TLC series, due to premiere on Nov. 10, Thore unveils her personal pad and its rainbow color palette for the first time while giving her friend and co-star Ashley Baynes a tour.

“I wanted it to be my dopamine apartment. You see how it’s colors, you see how it’s tchotchkes, you see how it’s fun?” asks Thore, as she points out the colorful mod decor she curated for the Queen City dwelling.

While Thore reports Beaudoin was immediately welcoming of the apartment’s playful style, she admits it’s been a challenge to accept his additions since moving in together.

“I don't love his stuff—that's the only issue—but luckily, he's cool with the aesthetic. It fits his vibe,” states Thore.

“It’s been very difficult to have a man in the apartment. ... I made him rent one of the storage units in the apartment for a lot of his stuff. I was basically like, ‘I don't want to see any evidence that you live here,’” she teases. She adds that they have made plans to "move out to a bigger place."

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Thore debuts the cheerfully decorated Charlotte dwelling where she’s found happiness, including the special living room nook she calls the most mood-boosting spot in her home.

When you walk in the door to this apartment, the view of uptown Charlotte through the windows is the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. It is exactly why I picked this apartment.

I feel instantly happy every time I walk in here. This is my favorite place I've ever lived, by miles. I really love what I've done in here.

When I moved to Charlotte, I wanted to feel creative. I was really moving here as a single girly—I didn't think that I was going to be dating anyone—and I wanted to make the space really conducive to feeling stimulated and creative.

I took a lot of liberties in this apartment that I would not do in my family home or in my Greensboro home where I felt like it has to be more grown-up or something like that. I [felt] the freedom to be like, “That's the cutest thing I've ever seen. I'm gonna get that, whether it fits or not.”

It's eclectic. It’s very funky. I have locker cabinets. There's a lot of texture and color, and it feels like motion to me. I have a lot of roundness and waviness: my coffee table, another table, my lamp, my candlesticks—I have a lot of shapes that I wouldn't normally have.

I have a lot of fun, whimsical things in this apartment, and I have a lot of color and a lot of art.

I am obsessed with [Henri] Matisse. I have, like, nine Matisse prints in here, and I even started doing art, which I hadn't done in almost 20 years. That was really exciting for me. I just wanted this space to feel bright and stimulating and exciting.

I have a lot of my own creations in here, things that I've drawn or done. Honestly, the thing I'm most proud of in this apartment is my little basketball gold net chain that I constructed. I got really into basketball when I moved to Charlotte. I started watching the Hornets and I got so into the season.  I don’t consider myself to be very crafty, [but] I ended up making a basketball net with chains and charms and I have that up.

I have a really cool digital picture of my mom that someone on the crew did for me. I have some little things of hers throughout the apartment that make me feel like she's here. I even have some of her handwritten notes on the refrigerator.

Just yesterday I found these glasses [for] $8. They’re like wrought iron. I reorganized ... to make room for the glasses. I'm still constantly picking and refining and moving things, and I'm just such a person that needs to feel so good in my physical space.

My physical space is such a representation of my mental space, so I can't have things super messy. I can't have things out of place.

In terms of the art and the shelving, I put a lot of work into making it fit me and my needs perfectly. I'm so particular and I like things done perfectly, measured perfectly, spaced perfectly.

I have ADHD, so I need little systems exactly how I need them to help me. If there's an extra step, then it's not going to happen.

I have a Russian handyman named Pavel. He is my lifesaver. Pavel and I have spent many, many hours together figuring out just how to make everything exactly how I wanted it, conducive to how I needed things. So no real renovations, but a lot of modifications.

Where I'm sitting right now is what I would consider [my sanctuary]. It's my armchair in the living room. It’s Ikea, so it's probably not real leather, but it's cognac. My rug is a beautiful bright blue; it’s not a pastel. The paint color is a light gray.

I like to read here. I can see straight out the window at night. The skyline and the view is so beautiful and soothing. I see the moon. I see Venus right outside my window. It gives me a peace that I usually experience in nature. I love this little corner where I look out the window, or I can watch TV, or do whatever. I spend a lot of my time out here just sitting.

I actually spend a lot of time in the apartment because I don't have a 9-to-5 job that brings me out of the apartment. That is one of the biggest reasons I've put so much into it and wanted to feel so comfortable in it, because I'm here all the time.

I don't often feel the need to even be out because where I live, you can see the skyline, there's life happening outside everywhere. There's always music, people. There's a train that goes by right outside my window. I feel like I can be in the safety and comfort of my home and still feel like I'm in the world, which is something that I would never have in Greensboro. That's something that I really missed. I felt very isolated and that I had to be out of the house to feel connected to the world. In Charlotte, I feel I'm part of it.

Charlotte really feels good to me. It really feels like home. I don't see myself leaving Charlotte in the next few years at least. I love the neighborhood that I live in. It's the same neighborhood that I lived in pre-COVID and during the beginning of COVID. It's a really wonderful mix of city life, and also, it’s still calm. It’s a really good fit for me and I love it here.

I really do feel like this specific apartment is such a big part of my experience in Charlotte. I'm very attached to it.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. Karli earned a BA in History from UCLA and an MA in Broadcast Journalism from San Francisco State University. She is equally grateful to have reported from both Hollywood red carpets and the comfort of her Bay Area home.

#5632. French blood banks hacked amid ‘deeply concerning’ wave of fridge and freezer cyberattacks in Europe

In a recent spate of cyberattacks in Europe against fridges and freezers, the latest assault hit France’s national blood service, where hackers gained control of cold storage systems at medical facilities and turned up the temperature.

The French Blood Establishment, EFS, told media that the facilities managed to save the blood supplies and there has been “no loss of blood products.” But the attacks come after supermarkets in several European countries experienced hacks of their fridges and freezers leading to the loss of millions of Euros in products.

Last month, hackers hit hundreds of supermarkets across France where temperatures were forced up to 50 degrees C overnight in what officials called an “unprecedented” attack. Food losses and fires were reported after “connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France.” What followed was a wave of similar attacks across the continent where fridges and freezers at stores in the U.K., Italy and Germany were recently hacked, following attacks in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously,” said EU Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

Connected fridges can now be controlled and monitored remotely through internet-connected software but with this comes vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit publicly reachable, legacy or unpatched remote refrigeration management controllers that may use default passwords or weak date-based administrative bypasses.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, told Reuters.

Cybersecurity experts so far have not figured out who’s behind the attacks. Russian hacking groups are a possibility as well as Iranian hacktivists or nation-state hackers. It might also be kids pulling off what have so far been very expensive pranks. Cybersecurity researchers at some firms have installed fake software as honeypots in an attempt to gather information about the hackers.

#5631. Generational Wealth Fuels Record-High Levels of Cash Sales Among First-Time Buyers

The share of first-time homebuyers paying all cash has climbed to record levels, fueled by generational wealth transfers, even as eroding affordability continues to push homeownership out of reach for many Americans.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 10% of rookie home shoppers paid all cash instead of relying on financing, marking the largest percentage on record, according to the annual Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors®.

The data also reveals that all-cash buyers were roughly three times likelier than financed first-time buyers to have used an inheritance (28% vs. 9%).

Across all first-time buyers—cash or financed—10% used an inheritance toward their home purchase, marking a new record and the fourth straight annual increase.

"The housing market is beginning to see a generational transfer of wealth. It’s not yet a tsunami, but it is changing who can buy a first home and when," says Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research. "Because people are living longer, the generation receiving that wealth isno longer young adults. Many are reaching middle age before they can buy their first home."

In fact, while the median age of first-time buyers held steady at a record high of 40, cash buyers skewed older, with the median age reaching 54 years old, compared to 38 for those who used financing.

Echoing Lautz, Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones confirms that the transfer of wealth from one generation to the next is starting to show up in the housing market, though the full effect won't likely be felt for a few more years.

Older homeowners hold substantial equity, and repeat buyers, with a median age of 62—matching a record high set last year— paid all cash 30% of the time in 2026. Jones says that for some rookie buyers, that wealth arrives as an inheritance.

"Buyers with access to inherited wealth have a significant advantage when they can purchase without financing," Anthony Mian, an agent with Douglas Elliman Beverly Hills, tells Realtor.com. "In multiple-offer situations, sellers often favor all-cash offers because they eliminate financing risk, reduce the likelihood of delays, and provide greater certainty of closing."

Other avenues open to baby boomers wishing to boost their children's or grandchildren's purchasing power include cash gifted toward a down payment, co-signing a loan, or selling investment properties, says Emilee Warner, a real estate agent at MW Real Estate Co. in Nashville, TN.

Looking at the top sources for a down payment among first-time buyers, personal savings continued to dominate (62%), followed by financial assets, such as 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency (30%), and gifts or loans from family and friends (25%).

"Wealth, whether built up or inherited, is increasingly what gets some buyers in, while buyers who depend on a mortgage still face high rates and prices," notes Jones.

Warner says she recently worked with first-time buyers who paid all cash borrowed the "bank" of mom and dad to purchase a home with a price tag exceeding $1 million.

"The cash buyers out there want to get in a home prior to rates dropping," Warner tells Realtor.com. "They are serious, willing, and able buyers. Cash allows appraisals to be waived, removing the risk of a low appraisal that could lose a financed buyer the home."

While more than half of repeat buyers (57%) relied on proceeds from the sale of their previous home and 42% used savings for their down payment, harnessing generational wealth among this cohort is not unheard of, with 4% using an inheritance or a gift from a family member or friend to fund their next home purchase.

Brandon Winn, an agent at Iowa Realty in Des Moines, IA, says he recently worked with move-up buyers who were purchasing a home with the help of their parents who offered them a 3% loan.

"This was when interest rates were 6.5%, and they gave them a 3% loan so they could afford to buy the home that they wanted," Winn tells Realtor.com.

Winn adds that at the luxury tier of the Des Moines market topping $600,000, he is seeing a growing number of buyers paying all cash using either inheritance or investment funds.

"Interest rates have risen so quickly that it's priced a lot of buyers out of the market," says the agent. "So if you have the cash ... it gives you the opportunity to purchase the house without having a [mortgage] payment, and then, of course, you're going to build equity quite a bit faster."

Mian, in Beverly Hills, says that for young families, that additional disposable income can go toward childcare, education, savings, or investments. Access to generational wealth can even expand their housing search geographically.

"In a market as expensive as Los Angeles, this can influence not only who can afford to purchase a home, but also which neighborhoods they can access and how much financial flexibility they retain after purchasing," he says. "Ultimately, generational wealth is becoming an important factor in determining both housing opportunities and long-term financial security."

Affordability continues to be the biggest major hurdle for aspiring U.S. homeowners.

The share of first-time buyers ticked up to 22% from last year's all-time low of 21%, yet it is still roughly half the historical norm of 40% recorded before 2008. Jones attributes the modest year-over-year boost to mortgage rate declines in the beginning of 2026.

Rates briefly dipped below 6% in February, before the outbreak of the Iran war, and were below year-ago levels from October 2025 through July 2026.

"This presented a window of opportunity for first-time buyers relying on a mortgage. The vast majority of first-time buyers financed their purchase, which means the median first-time buyer age is closer to the financed first-time buyer age," says Jones. "All-cash first-time buyers have aged 10 years in a decade, versus six for financed buyers, which shows they are a different group, middle-aged and drawing on savings, investments or inheritance."

Examining the makeup of first-time buyers in 2026, NAR data shows the share of first-time buyers who were married couples decreased slightly to 47%. Single women accounted for a quarter of all first-time buyers, same as in 2025, while the share of single men climbed to 12%, the highest level since 2011.

The typical novice buyer in 2026 had a median household income of $100,000, up from last year's $94,400.

The median down payment among first-time buyers this year was 9%, down from 10% in 2025 and significantly below the 18% recorded among all buyers.

As in years past, equity-rich repeat buyers continued to dominate the market, accounting for 78% of all home purchases with a median household income of $127,000 and a typical down payment of 19%— more than double that of first-timers. Nearly a third (30%) paid all cash.

"Repeat buyers are driving the housing market," says Lautz. "Unlike first-time home buyers, repeat buyers have seen their housing equity grow rapidly over the past decade, enabling them to trade up for larger homes or move into more desirable locations. These are often moves by choice rather than necessity."

The typical home seller in 2026 has owned their property for 12 years, a new all-time high surpassing last year's 11-year tenure. Forty-seven percent of sellers went on to purchase a newer home, and 36% bought a larger home.

Of all homes sold on the market, 78% did not have children under the age of 18 residing in the home, down from 81% last year.

For all sellers, the most commonly cited reason for selling their home was the desire to move closer to friends and family (22%), followed by the home being too small (12%), the home being too large (10%), a change in family situation (8%), and moving due to retirement (8%).

For recently sold homes, the final sales price was a median of 99% of the final listing price.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) led Tuesday’s withdrawals with $95 million in outflows. Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust lost another $52.6 million, adding to the pressure on the funds.

Several products still attracted fresh capital. Bitwise’s BITB recorded $21.9 million in inflows, while Fidelity’s FBTC added $6.8 million. Morgan Stanley’s MSBT also attracted $3.3 million.

The latest Bitcoin ETF data shows daily withdrawals falling by more than 80% from Friday’s peak. October also ended with roughly $515 million in net outflows, while November’s first three reported sessions added another $1.16 billion in withdrawals.

The slowdown offers a more encouraging signal for Bitcoin bulls, although the funds remain firmly in net-outflow territory. Institutional investors are still reducing exposure rather than rebuilding positions.

A return below $77,000 would expose the recent $75,600 low, where buyers previously stepped in.

The immediate outlook hinges on whether Bitcoin can turn $78,000 into support and challenge $80,000 with stronger buying volume. Slowing ETF withdrawals offer an encouraging backdrop, but a sustained move higher would require renewed spot demand rather than another short-lived relief rally.

#5629. Kyndryl shares surge 30% on hyperscaler-related revenue growth

Shares of Kyndryl Holdings Inc. jumped 30% today after it reported better-than-expected earnings for the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year.

Kyndryl generated $3.9 billion in sales during the three months ended Sept. 30. That represents a 1.9% decrease from a year earlier, but the company still managed to top the consensus estimate by about $50 million. It attributed the top-line surprise to its Kyndryl Consult business.

Kyndryl, a former IBM Corp. unit, once generated nearly all its revenue from managing other companies’ technology infrastructure. In 2022, it launched Kyndryl Consult to take on more strategic, higher-margin professional services deals.

The unit’s revenue grew 4.2% year-over-year in the second quarter. Kyndryl didn’t share a specific quarterly revenue number, but divulged that the unit earned a total of $3.6 billion over the past 12 months.

Kyndryl Consult’s signings, a measure of future revenue, jumped 19% over the past year. That momentum may have contributed to the company’s stock rally today.

Many of the projects that Kyndryl Consult takes on involve artificial intelligence. The unit can help customers build AI agent ensembles and set up training data generation pipelines. Additionally, it can advise clients about business decisions such as how they should allocate their AI budgets.

Kyndryl offers a software platform called Bridge to companies that buy its AI services. It enables AI agents to access business data from an organization’s internal systems. Additionally, Bridge monitors those agents to ensure they adhere to safety requirements.

The public cloud is another major focus of Kyndryl’s growth efforts. The company’s hyperscale-related revenue topped $500 million in the second quarter, which amounts to a 27% year-over-year increase.

“Strong signings and continued growth in Kyndryl Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue reinforce our confidence in our fiscal 2027 outlook,” said Kyndryl Chief Executive Officer Martin Schroeter. “Our performance reflects demand for Kyndryl’s AI-led modernization capabilities and deep mission-critical expertise that help customers evolve their complex technology environments, strengthen cybersecurity and achieve measurable business outcomes.”

The company delivered an adjusted net income of $92 million, which breaks down to 42 cents per share. Analysts expected 41 cents per share. The sum excludes a $38 million workforce reduction charge the company took in the second quarter. It’s part of a broader cost-cutting initiative that is set to save up to $500 million annually starting from Kyndryl’s 2028 fiscal year.

For the current fiscal year, the company is forecasting an adjusted pretax income of $600 million to $700 million. Kyndryl expects its revenue to be flat or increase by up to 2%.

#5628. Why the Garage Could Be a Home’s Biggest Flood Weak Spot

When homeowners think about protecting their property from flooding, the garage may not be the first place that comes to mind. But with its wide entrance, ground-level access and potential gaps around the door, a garage can be a vulnerable point when floodwater collects around a home.

A garage door’s bottom seal can help keep out everyday rain, leaves and debris, but it should not be assumed to provide reliable protection against floodwater. During periods of heavy rainfall, water may collect on a driveway, pool against the garage entrance or find its way through gaps around the door and threshold.

And the damage may not stop at a wet garage floor. Floodwater can affect vehicles, tools, appliances and stored belongings, while water entering through a connecting doorway may also threaten the rest of the house.

Cui Guanhong, flood barrier product specialist at Eudore, explains why homeowners should pay closer attention to their garages when preparing for flooding.

“Homeowners should consider the garage as part of their overall flood-prevention plan, rather than focusing only on front doors and windows,” he says. “The condition of the garage door seal, the height of the threshold and the way water moves across the driveway can all affect how vulnerable the entrance may be.”

Unlike a standard exterior door, a garage door often spans a wide opening close to ground level. This creates a larger area where water may enter if the door does not close properly or the surrounding surfaces allow water to accumulate.

“It’s worth checking what happens around the garage entrance during heavy rain,” says Cui. “If water consistently pools near the door, that is a sign to investigate the drainage and the way the driveway directs water.”

The bigger worry is often what is already inside the garage, starting with anything plugged in.

“The electrical risk comes first,” says Cui. “Outlets, extension cords, a chest freezer or a charger left plugged in can all become dangerous if floodwater reaches them.”

Official flood safety guidance from Ready.gov advises against touching electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Never enter a flooded garage or stand in water to reach electrical equipment or a breaker.

Garages may also contain water heaters and other heating equipment that could be damaged if floodwater reaches them. The extent of the damage depends on the equipment, its location and the depth of the water. Additionally, items stored at floor level, including power tools, paint cans, and cleaning products may be damaged or contaminated if floodwater enters the garage.

The connecting door is the part Cui believes homeowners underestimate most.

“If a garage opens directly into a hallway, laundry room, mudroom or kitchen, water entering the garage could potentially spread into the home,” he says. “Homeowners should consider this connection when assessing their property’s flood risk.”

Floor drains are the last detail, and the one that trips people up. During severe flooding, water may back up through floor drains if the drainage system becomes overwhelmed.

“Whether a backwater valve makes sense depends on how the property’s drainage is laid out, so that is a question for a qualified plumbing professional rather than a guess,” says Cui.

The best time to check your garage’s flood vulnerabilities is before a flood warning is issued. Waiting until water is already collecting outside the door may leave little time to inspect the entrance, install a barrier or move vulnerable belongings. Homeowners can start by checking their property’s flood risk, monitoring local weather alerts and preparing a plan for moving vehicles and important items to safer locations when necessary.

FEMA’s flood maps resources can help homeowners find official flood hazard information for their area, although a map should not be treated as a guarantee that a property will or will not flood.

It is also worth reviewing insurance arrangements before an emergency. Most standard homeowners insurance policies do not cover flood damage, so homeowners should check their policy and explore separate flood insurance if appropriate. FloodSmart, run by the National Flood Insurance Program, provides further information about flood insurance coverage and options.

Five ways to reduce a garage’s flood risk

Inspect the garage door seal. Check the bottom seal for cracks, gaps or signs of wear. Close the garage door and look for visible openings along the bottom and sides. Replace damaged seals in line with the manufacturer’s instructions. A sound seal can help limit ordinary water and debris entering through gaps, but it should not be treated as a substitute for flood protection.

Check the driveway and drainage. Observe where rainwater flows during a storm. Does it collect near the garage door, or does the driveway direct it towards the entrance? Keep drains and channels clear of leaves and debris. If water repeatedly pools around the garage, consider asking a qualified drainage or building professional to assess the slope and drainage arrangements. Any changes should be designed so they do not redirect water onto neighboring properties.

Consider a suitable flood barrier. Where flooding is a concern, a purpose-designed garage flood barrier may offer an additional layer of protection. However, not every barrier is suitable for every opening or flood scenario. Before choosing a product, check the dimensions of the garage entrance, the condition and level of the surfaces where the barrier will sit, and the manufacturer’s installation instructions and performance limitations. A barrier may be less effective if it is incorrectly fitted or used outside its specified conditions. Homeowners should also understand how quickly the barrier can be installed and where it will be stored so it can be accessed when needed.

Protect equipment and stored belongings. Where practical, keep valuable tools, electronics and important belongings off the garage floor. Use suitable shelving or storage that reduces the chance of items being damaged by shallow water. Store paints, fuels, cleaning products and other hazardous materials securely and in accordance with their labels. If electrical equipment, heating systems or other utilities could be exposed to floodwater, seek professional advice on appropriate protective measures.

Look at the route from the garage into your home. If your garage connects directly to your house, consider whether water entering the garage could reach the connecting doorway or adjoining rooms. The layout and floor levels of each property are different, so homeowners should avoid assuming that a simple DIY alteration will solve the problem. If flooding has affected the property before, a qualified building or flood-mitigation professional may be able to identify vulnerable entry points and appropriate improvements.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5627. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5623. Phaze raises $8.75M to give AI agents remote access to powerful workstations

If autonomous artificial intelligence agents are really going to become the future of the enterprise then they’re going to need to have a computer of their own so they can get on with their work without disturbing anyone else.

The founders of the remote desktop firm Parsec Technologies Inc. have come up with a new offering that’s designed to give those agents the computer access they need. Their new startup is called Phaze Inc., and it has just launched its offering after raising $8.75 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz. Today’s round also saw participation from Index, NextView, Makers and Lerer Hippeau.

Phaze has developed a high-performance remote desktop platform that’s designed to accommodate both humans and AI agent workers, giving them access to powerful computers, including high-end workstations. With its platform, those users can control a distant workstation with the same low-latency responsiveness and visual fidelity they’d get if they were accessing hardware locally.

The startup says it’s trying to solve a couple of glaring efficiency problems at many enterprises. One issue is the emergence of computer-use agents that like to hijack worker’s screens while automating mundane business tasks, reducing human productivity.

Another challenge is that many enterprises invest in powerful workstations capable of rendering complex 3D graphics and compiling massive codebases that can cost upwards of $10,000. Those machines are needed, but many information technology departments tend to have a policy of assigning one machine to each employee, which means that expensive hardware is often left sitting idle if that person goes out for lunch, sits in a meeting or takes a few days off.

Phaze’s solution is to transform those workstations into a shared pool of elastic compute, allowing anyone at an organization to access it via its proprietary low-latency streaming technology when they need it. This streaming tech is backed by a specially developed Model Context Protocol server that allows computer use agents to log into and operate expensive workstations the same way a human employee would.

The result: Instead of working exclusively through expensive and brittle application programming interfaces, agents can access a computer directly and navigate its operating system, launch applications and get work done.

Phaze co-founder and Chief Executive Benjy Boxer said the platform also supports human-to-agent collaboration, so they can work together to get more complex tasks done. For instance, an automated IT support bot might work to diagnose problems when new tickets are created, and then pass the session to a human engineer if the solution is more nuanced than what it’s authorized to do by itself.

“The computer sitting on your desk shouldn’t determine what compute you can access,” Boxer said. “People need powerful workstations to do their jobs, and now AI agents need computers they can actually operate. We’re building the access layer that lets either one connect to the machine they need, wherever it happens to be.”

By transforming expensive workstations into shared infrastructure, administrators can assign their computing resources dynamically to whoever needs access as people’s and agent’s workflows fluctuate. The workstations themselves can be sat on a desk, installed in a data center, or locked away in a cupboard. Wherever they’re located, organizations will be able to get maximum efficiency out of them.

Phaze’s job now is to convince enterprises of the benefits of its platform, and Boxer said the money from today’s round will be used to accelerate its go-to-market plans and onboard new customers. The startup will also look to expand its engineering team and develop more features.

Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado think Phaze is likely to see a lot of interest in its remote access platform, because workstations are too expensive to be left sitting idle for hours at a time. “Phaze is turning those machines into shared infrastructure for people and AI agents,” he said. “Benjy and the team have been building in this space for more than a decade and they bring that experience to a new era of remote access and machine management.”

#5622. Where Health Care Employment Has the Biggest Footprint

Health care is more than a service for residents. It is also an important piece of the employment landscape. Preliminary August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows significant differences in both the number of health care and social assistance jobs across states and the industry’s share of total employment.

In absolute terms, the country’s largest states naturally account for some of the biggest health care workforces. Unsurprisingly, California leads with over 3.18 million health care and social assistance jobs, followed by New York at 1.91 million and Texas at 1.76 million.

However, the health care industry’s share of a state’s total employment base may tell a different and potentially more useful story.

West Virginia stands at the top of the list, with health care and social assistance representing approximately 19.6% of total employment. New York follows at 19.1%, with Pennsylvania at 18.9%. Connecticut, Minnesota, and Massachusetts are also among the states where the industry accounts for a comparatively large share of employment, at roughly 18.1%, 17.9%, and 17.8%, respectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, health care represents just 8.8% of employment in Wyoming, 10.6% in the District of Columbia and Nevada, 10.8% in Alabama, and 11% in South Carolina.

That variation matters because a sizable health care sector can serve as an important economic anchor, providing a meaningful source of jobs that support the broader housing market.

Access to health care might become an increasingly relevant consideration in retirement location decisions. Affordability matters, but so do physician availability, provider access, and the distance residents need to travel for care.

Demographic trends reinforce that dynamic. Per the U.S. Census Bureau, the old-age dependency ratio, which measures the number of adults age 65+ relative to the working-age population, rose from 20.8 in 2010 to 29.7 in 2024, pointing to future pressure on health care systems, retirement programs, and elder care resources.

As the population ages, health care will matter to housing markets from both an economic and demographic perspective. The sector supports local employment, while access to care can influence where older households choose to live.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5621. Trend of the Month: 6 Ways Floor Plans Are Changing

Current floor plan trends don’t necessarily bring anything brand new to home design, but rather represent subtle shifts to better support how people want to live in their homes today.

Functionality and flow are driving many of the current trends, including these six:

As a result, floor plans are balancing the benefits of open-plan living with spaces that permit partial or total separation from the main living areas. Ideally, a floor plan lets a homeowner choose.

While the kitchen and adjacent living areas remain open, “what is changing is everything around that center. Homeowners still want visual generosity and togetherness, but they also need places for focused work, calls, study, rest, hobbies, or simply a quiet moment,” says Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture.

The key, says Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture, is not to treat open and closed spaces as opposites.

The most desirable plans “create layers between fully shared and fully enclosed space, so homeowners can adjust the degree of connection throughout the day,” says Julian.

Meanwhile, “Smaller cozy corners can remain open to the main space while using placement, furniture, partial screens, or an offset opening to create a sense of retreat,” says Wagner.

Away rooms are trending, which are simply secondary living spaces set off the main living area, with a closing door, and often increased soundproofing, devoted to peace and quiet.

Back kitchens and sculleries physically separate food prep, appliances and cleanup from the main kitchen, where much of daily living and entertaining takes place.

Upstairs retreats, homework rooms, and secondary living spaces create further separation, giving household members somewhere to do their own thing without sacrificing the openness of the kitchen and great room.

Wet rooms are not a new feature but are gaining more attention and are influencing bathroom layouts and design, no longer reserved just for higher-end homes.

“One reason is that you can use every inch of that space, which can mean a larger shower and a more spa-like feel,” says Debra Purvis with Design House.

A wet room typically is an open-concept bathroom, where a bathtub and a shower share an enclosure, sometimes separated by a glass partition from the rest of the bathroom.

Wet rooms offer great decorative potential too, with soaker tubs, steam showers, and statement fixtures. They also lend themselves naturally to other trends like tile drenching, which provides a dramatic, upscale look.

They are family friendly too. “Kids splash water out of the tub; it’s not a problem. Between the tile and floor drains, you are covered,” says Purvis.

Flex rooms offer opportunity in a floor plan without adding square footage, one reason they remain among the most sought-after features in new homes. But today’s buyers are looking for flex rooms with purpose, rather than just a blank-slate bonus room.

Practical considerations, such as outlets, storage, layered lighting, and easy access without crossing through other spaces, offer flexible futureproofing. The flex room needs to be appropriately sized and configured for the potential use too.

Location in the home indicates flex room potential too.

While two-story floor plans remain in-demand, one-story floor plans are showing modest growth.

“A one-story plan is going to be more accessible, generally speaking, which opens it up to buyers in many different life phases,” says Aurora Zeledon, director of digital content and marketing for Zonda House Plans, including Houseplans.com.

While land availability and cost might be driving the uptick in one-story floor plans, the versatility of living on one level has design upside and broad-based appeal, including 55+, multigen households, and younger families who appreciate having everyone on the same level.

One-story plans offer easier circulation, without stairs and landings occupying transitional spaces. Typically, one-story homes benefit from a stronger indoor/outdoor connection, often an anchor of the design, an in-demand feature as well.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), two-story plans still accounted for over half of single-family home starts in 2025 nationwide, although that number had dropped slightly, while the number of single-story homes inched up. Notably, there were significant differences across regions.

Meanwhile, Zeledon reports that the majority of floor plans they have sold, dating back to 2019, are for one-story homes, including their current bestseller. However, she notes that year-to-date there has been a modest increase in one-story house plan sales, compared to last year, pointing out that much of the activity is concentrated in the South and Southeast.

As homes generally scale down in size, storage becomes essential for homeowners to retain the functionality of a larger home in a smaller footprint.

“The overarching idea is to utilize every square foot. When storage is thoughtfully integrated into the architecture, we can maximize the home for multiple purposes—and, importantly, multiple storage solutions—without making the spaces feel overly utilitarian,” says Hannah Sloan, creative marketing specialist with Unscripted Interior Design.

She reports that drop zones are gaining attention, as are Costco closets, laundry/mudroom and owner’s entrances.

Sloan says that some rooms are benefiting from space-specific storage that improves functionality, like in the primary bathroom with more thoughtfully designed vanities and built-ins. Meanwhile, fitness closets are appearing in home gyms to free up floor space for exercise.

“Then there are the found spaces—under-stair book nooks, hidden speakeasy-inspired bars, and other whimsical design opportunities. These spaces can become highly functional while also adding personality and surprise to a home,” says Sloan.

#5620. The Home Depot Foundation Expands Veteran Housing Commitment to $1 Billion

The Home Depot Foundation is increasing its total commitment to veteran causes to $1 billion through 2032, expanding investments in programs designed to address veteran homelessness, housing insecurity, and home accessibility.

Since 2011, the foundation says it has invested more than $650 million in veteran causes and helped improve more than 70,000 veteran homes and facilities. Its latest commitment will combine established housing programs with efforts to test and scale new approaches to veteran housing.

“We believe every veteran deserves a safe place to call home,” said Erin Izen, executive director of The Home Depot Foundation. “Our $1 billion commitment supports the partnerships and solutions needed to help more veterans move from uncertainty to long-term stability.”

Among the initiatives receiving support are programs designed to remove barriers to rental housing. The foundation is also investing in homelessness prevention and permanent supportive housing through organizations including Operation Homefront and Community Solutions. Additional funding will explore alternative housing approaches, including modular homes from Purple Heart Homes for senior veterans and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

The announcement coincides with the foundation’s annual Celebration of Service. This fall, Team Depot, The Home Depot’s associate volunteer force, is expected to complete hundreds of projects benefiting veterans across all 50 states and three U.S. territories.

One recent project brought The Home Depot Foundation, Team Depot, and Purple Heart Homes together to construct a fully accessible modular home on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., for James “Jim” Taylor, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran who previously experienced homelessness.
